questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A diabetic patient was advised exercise by the treating physician. The glucose transporter which is insulin sensitive is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glut 4

GLUT-4 is the insulin-sensitive glucose transporter, primarily found in:

• Skeletal muscle
• Adipose tissue

Mechanism:

• In response to insulin, GLUT-4 translocates from intracellular vesicles to the cell membrane
• This increases glucose uptake into cells
• Exercise can also stimulate GLUT-4 translocation independent of insulin

Clinical relevance in diabetes:

• Exercise improves glucose uptake even when insulin action is impaired
• Hence, exercise is beneficial in diabetes management

Why other options are incorrect:

• GLUT-1: RBCs, brain (insulin-independent)
• GLUT-2: Liver, pancreas (high Km, bidirectional)
• GLUT-3: Neurons (high affinity, insulin-independent)

questions.text: Which of the following equations is used to determine the pH of a buffer solution?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Henderson–Hasselbalch equation

The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is used to calculate the pH of a buffer solution based on the ratio of a weak acid and its conjugate base.

This equation explains how blood pH is maintained by the balance between bicarbonate (kidneys) and CO₂ (lungs).

Other equations:

A. Nernst equation: Calculates equilibrium potential of ions across membranes.

B. Goldman equation: Determines membrane potential considering multiple ions.

C. Gibbs–Donnan equation: Describes ion distribution across membranes with impermeant charged molecules.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Name the surgical procedure in which the instrument shown below is used?
questions.explanation: The instrument shown is a bone-biting punch (specifically a Citelli or Hajek punch), which is an essential tool in Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR). During a DCR, the surgeon must remove a portion of the lacrimal bone and the frontal process of the maxilla to create an ostium (opening) into the nasal cavity. This punch is designed specifically to clip away these small sections of bone safely. Evisceration (Option A) and Enucleation (Option B) are procedures to remove the internal contents or the entirety of the globe, respectively; these surgeries involve scalpels, scissors, and distractors, not specialized bone-biting punches. Cataract surgery (Option C) is a microscopic intraocular procedure utilizing fine forceps and phacoemulsification probes rather than heavy orthopedic-style tools. Therefore, because the creation of a bony window is the defining mechanical step of DCR, the bone-biting punch is definitively associated with that procedure. Recognizing specialized instrumentation is a core skill in surgical clinical examinations

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which ganglion is located in the area indicated in the image?
questions.explanation: The image indicates the infratemporal fossa, specifically the region just below the foramen ovale. The otic ganglion is a small parasympathetic ganglion located in this area, immediately below the foramen ovale and medial to the mandibular nerve. It serves as a relay station for secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland. The ciliary ganglion (Option B) is located within the orbit, posterior to the eyeball. The pterygopalatine ganglion (Option C) resides in the pterygopalatine fossa, accessible through the sphenopalatine foramen. The submandibular ganglion (Option D) is located on the hyoglossus muscle, suspended from the lingual nerve. The otic ganglion receives preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the lesser petrosal nerve (a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve). Postganglionic fibers then travel via the auriculotemporal nerve to stimulate the parotid gland. Precise knowledge of these cranial nerve ganglia and their locations is fundamental for diagnosing various autonomic dysfunctions in the head and neck region

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient's relatives sent a message on social media to the consulting doctor, unaware about the other investigations. But he mentioned that urinary coproporphyrin is positive. What is the probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lead poisoning

Lead poisoning interferes with heme synthesis, leading to accumulation of porphyrin precursors such as coproporphyrin in urine. Lead inhibits key enzymes in the heme pathway:

• ALA dehydratase (ALAD)
• Ferrochelatase

Consequences:

• ↑ ALA and coproporphyrin in urine
• ↓ heme synthesis → anemia

Clinical features:

• Abdominal pain (lead colic)
• Neurological symptoms (irritability, neuropathy)
• Anemia with basophilic stippling
• Wrist/foot drop

Why other options are incorrect:

• Asbestosis: Lung fibrosis (no effect on heme synthesis)
• Silicosis: Occupational lung disease
• Mercury poisoning: Neurological and renal toxicity, not porphyrin metabolism

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a known history of rheumatic heart disease is found on imaging to have an aneurysm measuring 1–2 cm. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: A coronary artery aneurysm measuring 1–2 cm (10–20 mm) is classified as a large aneurysm. Such lesions carry a high risk of complications, including intraluminal thrombosis and distal embolization, which can lead to myocardial infarction. The standard of care for long-term thrombotic risk reduction in these patients is lifelong low-dose aspirin therapy. Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with Clopidogrel (Option B) is typically reserved for acute coronary syndromes or giant aneurysms rather than stable large ones. A 3-week course of aspirin (Option C) is insufficient because the risk of clot formation persists as long as the aneurysm is present. IV antibiotics (Option D) are only indicated if there is evidence of an infected (mycotic) aneurysm or active endocarditis. Thus, permanent antiplatelet protection is the cornerstone of management

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient was brought to the hospital after a road traffic accident. He had severe muscle injury. ECG is shown here. What change will happen to the resting membrane potential in this patient?
options: First becomes more positive, then negative
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Becomes more positive

Severe muscle injury (rhabdomyolysis) releases K⁺ into the blood → hyperkalemia (ECG classically shows tall peaked T waves, widening QRS in severe cases). Increased extracellular K⁺ reduces the K⁺ gradient, so less K⁺ leaves the cell, making the resting membrane potential less negative (more positive/depolarized).

A. No change / B. more negative – seen with hypokalemia (more negative).

D. First becomes more positive, then negative – not the typical physiologic sequence in hyperkalemia.
questions.learning: Becomes more positive Severe muscle injury (rhabdomyolysis) releases K⁺ into the blood → hyperkalemia (ECG classically shows tall peaked T waves, widening QRS in severe cases).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient with known hyperthyroidism who is not receiving treatment is scheduled for a total thyroidectomy. Pre-anesthetic evaluation has been inadequately performed. What is the most serious complication that is most likely to occur during surgery?
options: Hypothyroidism (C) Arrhythmia In a patient with uncontrolled hyperthyroidism, the body is in a hypermetabolic state with significantly increased sensitivity to catecholamines. Surgical stress or manipulation of the thyroid gland can precipitate a life-threatening "thyroid storm" (thyrotoxic crisis). The most immediate and dangerous intraoperative manifestation of this crisis is severe cardiac arrhythmia, such as atrial fibrillation or supraventricular tachycardia. While hyperthermia (Option A) is a classic sign of thyroid storm, arrhythmias pose a more acute threat to hemodynamic stability during the procedure. Hypothermia (Option B) is generally associated with prolonged surgery in cold environments, not thyrotoxicosis. Hypothyroidism (Option D) is an expected long-term consequence of a total thyroidectomy but would not occur as an acute intraoperative complication. Therefore, managing heart rate and rhythm via preoperative beta-blockade and antithyroid medications is essential to prevent these intraoperative cardiac emergencies.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Roth spots are seen in ________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute leukemia

Roth's spots are seen in acute leukemia.

Roth's spots are retinal hemorrhages with white or pale center. The white centre due to coagulated fibrin-platelet plug is surrounded by red rim that is caused by hemorrhage.  Roth's spots may be seen in:

1. Subacute bacterial endocarditis
2. Leukemia
3. Diabetes
4. Sickle cell retinopathy
5. Hypertensive retinopathy
6. HIV retinopathy
7. Systemic lupus erythematosus

The fundus image below shows Roth's spots.

Option B: Uveal melanoma devolps due to malignant transformation of the normal melanocytes present in the uveal tissue. Primary posterior uveal melanoma (choroidal melanoma) which forms the majority of uveal melanoma manifests as:

• A solitary elevated subretinal grey-brown dome shaped mass
• "Collar stud" appearance on B-scan - when the tumor breaks through the Bruchs membrane and protrudes into subretinal space
• "Double circulation" sign

Primary anterior uveal melanoma frequently involves the iris and presents as nodular melanocytic mass on the iris. The below given fundus image shows the "double circulation sign" of choroidal melanoma.

Option C: Uveal lymphoma is characterized by localized or diffuse uveal infiltrates of malignant lymphoma cells. Fundus examination in these patients show diffuse creamy thickening of posterior uvea with nodular accentuation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Paris green dust is used to eliminate the larval form of _________________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anopheles

Paris green is a commonly used larvicide agent against surface feeders like Anopheles larvae.

Paris green (Copper acetoarsenite) is an insecticide, which is a green powder that has 50% arsenious oxide. It is a stomach poison and to be effective, it must be ingested by the larvae.

The larvae of Anopheles are surface feeders as they lie parallel to the surface of the water due to the absence of a siphon tube. In contrast, Culicine larvae like Aedes, Culex, and Mansonia have a siphon tube that helps them to suspend in water with their head downwards and therefore not affected by pair green.

The image below shows Laraval forms of different mosquitoes.

Other commonly used larvicides include:

* Mineral oils - diesel oil, kerosene, fractions of crude oils, mosquito larvicidal oil

* Synthetic insecticides - Fenthion, Chlorpyrifos, and Abat

Larvicides that are not recommended include organochlorine compounds like DDT (Dichloro-diphenyl-trichloroethane)and HCH (hexachlorocyclohexane). This is because they have a long residual effect, and contaminate water. Vector mosquitoes may also develop resistance to these compounds.

Pearl PF1010: Mosquito Control Measures

Mosquito Control Measures

* Anti-larval measures

* Environmental control

* This is done by source reduction by eliminating breeding places through appropriate methods for the different species.

* Intermittent irrigation is also a method of environmental control

* Chemical control

* Mineral oils: Oldest known larvicidal method. Oils that are used are diesel oil, kerosene, crude oil fractions. Disadvantage is that it kills fish.

* Paris green: Copper acetoarsenite is an emerald green, micro-crystalline powder and is insoluble in water. It is a stomach poison to larvae. It is not harmful to man or animals. Very effective against Anopheles as they are surface feeders.

* Synthetic insecticides: Organo-phosphorous compounds like fenthion, chlorpyrifos and abate are larvicidal. Abate is least toxic.

* Biological control

* The fish species Gambusia affinis and Lebister reticulatus (Barbados millions) feed on mosquito larvae.

* These are used in conjunction with other methods.

* Anti-adult measures

* Residual sprays

* Adult mosquitoes can be controlled by spraying with residual insecticides like DDT, Malathion, propoxur and gamma-HCH (lindane)

* Resistance to DDT has been shown by mosquitoes

* Space sprays

* Space sprays are those in which insecticides are sprayed into the atmosphere in the form of a mist or fog.

* Pyrethrum is a contact, nerve poison and is the most common insecticide used as a space spray. Its active principle is pyrethrin.

* Ultra-low volume space spraying (ULV) is done with Malathion and fenitrothion.

* Genetic control by sterile male technique, cytoplasmic incompatibility, sex distortion, etc.

* Protection against bites

* Usage of mosquito nets, building screens and repellants like diethyltoluamide (deet), indalone, dimethylphthalate, dimethyl carbate, etc.

Pearl PF1014: Insecticides

Contact poisons

* Natural: Pyrethrum, rotenone, derris, nicotine, mineral oils

* Synthetic:

* Organo-chlorine compounds: DDT, methoxychlor, HCH, lindane, chlordane, heptachlor, dieldrin, aldrin, toxaphene, kepone, mirex.

* Repellants: Benzyl benzoate, indalone, meta-diethyltoluamide, dimethyl phthalate, ethyl hexanediol.

* Organo-phosphorus compounds: Chlorthion (aryl), diazinon (aryl), demethoate, malathion (alkyl), fenthion, parathion (aryl), trichlorfon (alkyl), runnel, abale, naled, chlorpyrifos, fenitrothion, dicapthon.

* Carbamates: Carbaryl, dimetilan, propoxur, pyrolan.

* Synthetic pyrethroids: Prothrin, resmethrin, bioresmethrin, permethrin, proparthin, tetramethrin

* Stomach poisons: Paris green, sodium fluoride.

* Fumigants: Hydrogen cyanide, methyl bromide, sulphur dioxide, carbon disulphide.

Specific Insecticides
Comments

DDT (Dichloro-diphenyl-thrichloroethane)
Insecticidal properties were discovered by Swiss scientist, Paul Muller. Most widely used insecticide. Attacks nerves of insects but doesn’t cause immediate death. White amorphous powder. Contains 70 – 80% of para-para isomers, which is the most active fraction of DDT. Has residual action up to 18 months. Used as a residual spray.Least toxic organo-chlorine compound.

HCH (hexachlorocyclo-hexane)
Synthesized by Michael Faraday. Normal HCH contains 13 – 16% of gamma isomer. Gamma-HCH or lindane has 99% gamma isomer.Short residual action – 3 months.

Malathion
Least toxicity of all organophosphorus compounds. Used as an ultra-low volume spray.

Fenthion
Also called baytex. Used as a residual spray.

Pyrethrum
Vegetable origin – Chrysanthemum cinerariafolium. Nerve poison and is excellent as a space spray.No residual action.Synergistic action with DDT as space spray.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
Which of the following statements is true about palliative care?

A. Disease is the centre of concern
B. The patient is sovereign
C. Death should neither be prolonged nor hastened
D. The aim is to improve the quality of life
E. The intention is to cure
F. Imperative to do something than passively observe
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. B,D

True statements are:

• The patient is sovereign
• The aim is to improve the quality of life

Palliative care helps patients and their families cope with physical, psychological, social, and spiritual obstacles of life-threatening disease. It is interesting to note that even the quality of life of the caregiver also improves. Palliative care is needed by 56.8 million individuals annually, including 25.7 million in their final year according to WHO, while only 14% of palliative care patients worldwide receive it.

Palliative care improves the quality of life of life-threatening illness patients and their families. Early detection, assessment, and treatment of physical, psychosocial, and spiritual suffering and additional concerns diminish discomfort. Addressing suffering goes beyond physical symptoms. Palliative care supports patients and caregivers collaboratively. This includes practical assistance and bereavement counselling. It supports patients to live as fully as possible till death.

The human right to health includes palliative care. Patient-centred and integrated health services should focus on individual needs and preferences.

Many diseases require palliative care. Most palliative care patients have chronic conditions like cardiovascular disease (38.5%), cancer (34%), respiratory disease (10.3%), AIDS (5.7%), and diabetes (4.6%). Kidney failure, chronic liver illness, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's, rheumatoid arthritis, neurological disease, dementia, congenital defects, and drug-resistant TB may require palliative care.

Most common and serious symptoms that patients undergoing palliative care experience are pain and respiratory difficulties. Almost 80% of AIDS, cancer, and 67% of cardiovascular and COPD patients would experience moderate to severe agony at death.

Opioids also relieve dyspnea and diminish the increased pain experienced by patients. Early symptom control is ethical to reduce suffering and respect the dignity of the patient.
questions.learning: B,D True statements are: • — The patient is sovereign • The aim is to improve the quality of life Palliative care helps patients and their families cope with physical, psychological, social, and spiritual obstacles of life-threatening disease.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the immediate next step in the management of a 29-week gestation infant with a heart rate of less than 100/min and an oxygen saturation of 80% in the right upper limb?
options: Positive pressure ventilation with room air
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Positive pressure ventilation with 21-30% O2

The immediate next step in managing a 29-week preterm neonate with a heart rate <100/min and SpO₂ of 80% in the right upper limb is positive pressure ventilation (PPV) with a bag and mask using 21–30% oxygen.

According to the Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP) guidelines, management is based on heart rate (HR) and oxygen saturation (SpO₂) targets:

* HR <100/min → Initiate PPV (Key indicator for respiratory distress or inadequate breathing).

* SpO₂ at 80% in the first few minutes is slightly low but within the normal transitional range for preterm infants. However, ventilation support is needed since HR is <100/min.

* Preterm infants (≤35 weeks gestation) should receive initial PPV with 21–30% oxygen (not 100%) to minimize oxidative injury.

* If HR remains <60/min despite effective PPV, chest compressions and higher FiO₂ (up to 100%) should be considered.

As soon as a baby is born, the tone, cry, breathing efforts, and respiratory efforts are assessed. If the tone is poor, or if the baby is not breathing, the following measures are done immediately - warming to maintain the normal temperature, proper positioning of the baby's airway, i.e. sniffing position with the head slightly extended, clearing of airway secretions, and tactile stimulation.

After the initial steps of neonatal resuscitation, the heart rate of the baby must be assessed. If the heart rate is < 100 beats per minute (bpm), positive pressure ventilation is provided along with SPO2 monitoring to ensure adequate ventilation.

If the heart rate remains at < 100 bpm, ventilation corrective steps and/or endotracheal intubation have to be considered. The ventilation corrective steps are as follows and can be remembered with the mnemonic MRSOPA.

* Mask has to be reapplied

* Reposition head

* Suction the secretions

* Open mouth slightly and ventilate

* Pressure is increased slightly

* Airway may be changed

If the heart rate is < 60 bpm, chest compressions are initiated over the lower third of the sternum at a rate of 90 compressions/min. The ratio of compressions to ventilation is 3: 1 (90 compressions: 30 breaths).

If the heart rate still remains <60 bpm, despite effective compressions and ventilation, then epinephrine (1:10,000 solution at 0.1–0.3 mL/kg intravenously or 0.5–1 mL/kg intratracheally) should be administered. The dosage can be repeated every 3–5 minutes. Persistent bradycardia may signify inadequate ventilation or severe cardiac compromise.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is true regarding genital tuberculosis?
options: The most common site of affection is ovary.
Abdominal ostium is closed in tobacco pouch appearance.
The most common mode of spread from primary to genital organs is haematogenous.
Genital tuberculosis occurs in 1–2% of patients who had pulmonary tuberculosis in adolescence.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The most common mode of spread from primary to genital organs is haematogenous.

• A. The most common site of affection is ovary: Incorrect. The fallopian tubes are the most commonly affected site in female genital tuberculosis, not the ovary.
• B. Abdominal ostium is closed in tobacco pouch appearance: Incorrect. In tuberculous salpingitis, the abdominal ostium may be blocked, producing a tobacco-pouch appearance due to a distended, club-shaped tube. The statement as worded is not the best description of the classic finding.
• C. The most common mode of spread from primary to genital organs is haematogenous: Correct. Genital TB usually results from hematogenous spread from a primary focus, commonly pulmonary TB.
• D. Genital tuberculosis occurs in 1–2% of patients who had pulmonary tuberculosis in adolescence: Incorrect. Genital TB is not limited to 1–2% of patients with adolescent pulmonary TB; the association is considerably more complex.
questions.learning: The most common mode of spread from primary to genital organs is haematogenous. • A. The most common site of affection is ovary: Incorrect.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A male patient presents with hydrophobia, tearing, and altered sensorium after a dog bite. You suspect rabies in this patient and take corneal scrapings to confirm the same. What test is performed to obtain the most accurate diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reverse transcription-PCR for virus

Detection of rabies virus RNA by RT-PCR(reverse transcriptase -polymerase chain reaction) on corneal scrapings is highly sensitive and specific.

This technique can detect viruses in fresh saliva samples, CSF, skin, and brain tissues. RT-PCR with genetic sequencing can distinguish among rabies variants, permitting identification of the probable source of an infection.

Laboratory diagnosis of rabies is performed by the following methods:

* Antigen detection - Direct immunofluorescence (IF) from specimens of

* Skin biopsy from the nape of the neck including hair follicles. Rabies antigen is present in cutaneous nerves at the base of hair follicles. It is the most sensitive and specific test.

* Corneal smears were previously used. They are not used anymore as they are of low diagnostic yield.

* Viral isolation- Intracerebral inoculation in mice can be attempted from the brain, CSF, and saliva

* Antibody demonstration from serum and CSF

* Viral RNA detection by RT-PCR

* Postmortem examination of brain tissue samples- demonstration of Negri bodies

Pearl PF1934: Rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins schedules

According to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India:

WHO category II or III exposures should receive post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) immediately.

One intradermal (ID) dose is 0.1 mL of vaccine and one intramuscular (IM) dose is an entire vial of vaccine, irrespective of the vial size.

Should a vaccine dose be delayed for any reason, the PEP schedule should be resumed (not restarted).

Rabies Immunoglobulin(RIG):

* Passive immunization

* Single-dose; after initiation of PEP and not beyond 7 days after the first dose of vaccine

* Max dose: hRIG - 20IU/kg , eRIG - 40IU/kg body weight

* Vaccines should never be withheld regardless of the availability of RIG.

* Alternatives for RIG- WHO recommends monoclonal antibodies (mAb) as a 'cocktail' containing at least two antibodies against the rabies virus.

Administration of RIG:

* RIG should be administered into or around the wound site or sites.

* The remaining RIG, if any, should be injected IM at a site distant from the site of vaccine administration.

* RIG may be diluted to a volume sufficient for all wounds to be effectively and safely infiltrated.

Prioritization of RIG allocation (numbered according to priority order):

* Multiple bites

* Deep wounds

* Bites to head, neck, and hands

* Patients with severe immunodeficiency

* Confirmed/probable rabies in biting animal

* Bites, scratches, and exposure of mucous membranes caused by a bat

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)

PrEP is considered in the following conditions:

* High-risk groups- laboratory staff, wildlife wardens, veterinarians, animal handlers, and travelers to endemic regions.

* Remote, rabies-endemic areas where access to PEP is difficult

* Areas where dog bite incidence is >5% per year

* Areas where vampire bat rabies is known to be present.

Pre-exposure rabies vaccination consists of two intramuscular (IM) or two intradermal (ID) doses. These are given on days 0 and 3.

* Adults - the vaccine should always be administered in the deltoid area of the arm

* Young children (under 1 year of age)- Administration into the anterolateral area of the thigh is recommended.

* Rabies vaccine should never be administered in the gluteal area. Administration in this manner will result in lower neutralizing antibody titers.

For exposed or re-exposed patients who can document previous completion of PEP the following guidelines would be applicable:

* Proper wound management should be done.

* There is no need for the administration of RIG.

* One site ID or IM vaccine administration on days 0 and 3.

Only adequate wound washing would be required in case of re-exposure where the animal bite victim has documented proof of complete PEP within the last three months.

The following cases are treated as fresh cases and given full PEP:

* Those who have previously received full post-exposure treatment with neural tissue vaccines (NTV) or vaccines of unproven potency

* Those who cannot document complete PEP or PrEP treatment

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 52-year-old carpenter presents with the history of a persistent non-healing ulcer on his lower alveolus. He is a smoker for last 30 years and also chews tobacco. What is the next most appropriate step in the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Edge biopsy of ulcer

A persistent non-healing ulcer of the lower alveolus in a long-term smoker and tobacco chewer is highly suspicious for oral squamous cell carcinoma.

The next appropriate step is biopsy, preferably an incisional biopsy from the edge of the ulcer, including the transition between normal and abnormal tissue.

• A. X-ray mandible: May be performed later to assess bony involvement, but it does not establish the diagnosis.
• B. Edge biopsy: Correct. Provides tissue for histopathological confirmation of malignancy.
• C. Local gum paint: Inappropriate when malignancy is suspected.
• D. Systemic antibiotics: Not indicated unless there is evidence of superimposed infection.
questions.learning: Edge biopsy of ulcer — A persistent non-healing ulcer of the lower alveolus in a long-term smoker and tobacco chewer is highly suspicious for oral squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-year-old child is brought with a lesion involving the right eye. Histopathological examination shows Flexner–Wintersteiner rosettes. Based on this finding, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presence of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes on histopathological examination is pathognomonic for Retinoblastoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood. These rosettes consist of a ring of columnar tumor cells surrounding a central lumen, representing an attempt at retinal differentiation. Clinically, retinoblastoma characteristically presents in a young child (most often before age 5) with leukocoria (a white pupillary reflex or "cat's eye" reflex) and occasionally strabismus. Optic nerve glioma (Option B) is a tumor of the nerve itself, not the retina. Rhabdomyosarcoma (Option C) is the most common primary orbital malignancy in children but does not originate within the eye. Ocular melanoma (Option D) is the most common primary eye cancer in adults, not children. Early diagnosis of retinoblastoma is critical to save both the life and the vision of the child. Treatment modalities include chemotherapy, cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, and enucleation in advanced cases
questions.learning: The presence of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes on histopathological examination is pathognomonic for Retinoblastoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which is the anaesthesia of choice in a day care dental surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Infiltration anesthesia

Infiltration anesthesia is ideal to perform in day care dental procedures as a fast-track procedure.

It has a lesser incidence of complications than regional or general anesthesia. Other anesthetic techniques for hernia repair include intercostal block and ilioinguinal nerve block.

Ambulatory/Outpatient anesthesia employs the use of fast - Track surgical techniques to provide adequate surgical anesthesia and minimize post-operative complications in order to reduce the duration of hospital stay.

Disadvantage of infiltration anesthesia - Short duration of anesthesia even when long-acting local anesthetics like bupivacaine are used. Extended- duration local anesthesia can be produced by encapsulating bupivacaine into a biodegradable carrier.

Regional anesthesia is contraindicated in patients with bleeding disorders, those on anticoagulants and with local infections.

Spinal anesthesia has the disadvantage over epidural anesthesia of delayed recovery due to profound motor blockade. Spinal opioids like fentanyl or sufentanil are added to prolong postoperative analgesia and minimize motor block without delaying recovery. But the adverse effects of spinal opioids like nausea, pruritus and postoperative urinary retention are additive.
questions.learning: Infiltration anesthesia Infiltration anesthesia is ideal to perform in day care dental procedures as a fast-track procedure. It has a lesser incidence of complications than regional or general anesthesia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which medication is the treatment of choice for Legionnaires disease?
questions.explanation: Legionnaires' disease is a severe form of pneumonia caused by Legionella pneumophila, which is an atypical, intracellular pathogen. Azithromycin (a macrolide) is currently the first-line treatment of choice due to its high intracellular penetration, superior efficacy, and better safety profile compared to older agents. Respiratory fluoroquinolones like levofloxacin are also considered first-line. Vancomycin (Option A) is used for MRSA and has no activity against Legionella. Streptomycin (Option C) is an aminoglycoside used primarily for tuberculosis. Erythromycin (Option D) was historically the first-line treatment, but it is now less preferred because of a higher incidence of gastrointestinal side effects and the need for more frequent dosing compared to the modern macrolide, azithromycin. Therefore, given its pharmacokinetic advantages and clinical success, azithromycin is the definitive treatment of choice for patients with this specific infection

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A family that consumes a diet predominantly consisting of polished rice develops symptoms of muscle weakness and difficulty in movement. Which of the following nutrients should be administered as prophylaxis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thiamine

A diet predominantly consisting of polished rice lacks thiamine (vitamin B1) because the polishing process removes the outer bran layer, which contains most of the thiamine. Deficiency of thiamine leads to beriberi, characterized by muscle weakness, neuropathy, and difficulty in movement due to impaired energy production in nerve and muscle cells.

Thiamine acts as an essential cofactor for enzymes involved in carbohydrate metabolism, including pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase. When thiamine is deficient, ATP production decreases, particularly affecting tissues with high energy demand such as nervous tissue and muscles, resulting in neuromuscular symptoms.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Calcium: Deficiency mainly causes bone disorders such as osteopenia or osteoporosis.
• Vitamin D: Deficiency leads to rickets or osteomalacia, not primarily neuromuscular weakness related to polished rice diets.
• Iron: Deficiency causes anemia rather than neuropathy or movement difficulty.
questions.learning: Thiamine — A diet predominantly consisting of polished rice lacks thiamine (vitamin B1) because the polishing process removes the outer bran layer, which contains most of the thiamine.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the fluid shown below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ringer lactate

The fluid shown in the image is ringer lactate or Hartmann's solution.

Ringer lactate, or Hartmann's solution, is a crystalloid made up of sodium 131 mEq, chloride 112 mEq, potassium 5 mEq, bicarbonate (as lactate) 29 mEq, and 2 mEq of calcium. It is devoid of glucose.

It is useful in the following conditions:

• Correction of severe hypovolemia
• Metabolic acidosis
• Postoperative period, burns, diarrhea
• Correction of hypokalemia
• Diabetic ketoacidosis.

It should be avoided in severe shock, liver diseases, vomiting, nasogastric aspiration, and metabolic alkalosis. It cannot be used along with blood transfusion since calcium in the ringer lactate can bind with citrate in the transfused blood leading to clot formation.

Other options:

Option A: Haemaccel is a colloid and contains 145 mmol of sodium, 6.25 mmol of calcium, and 5.1 mmol of potassium. It is mainly used for rapid volume replacement in circulatory shock, burns, and trauma. These release histamine and hence, H2 blocker has to be supplemented. It is also used in heart-lung machines.

Options C and D: Isolyte P and Isolyte M are crystalloids. Isolyte P is commonly used in fluid therapy for pediatrics. One liter contains 50 grams of glucose, 25 mEq of sodium, 22 mEq of potassium, 3 mEq of magnesium, and 23 mEq of acetate. Hyponatremia, renal failure, hyperkalemia, and hypovolemic shock are some of the contraindications.
Isolyte M is used for maintenance. It mainly contains 50 grams of glucose, 40 mEq sodium, 38 mEq chloride, 35 mEq potassium, 15 mEq phosphate, and 20 mEq acetate. It is useful in correcting hypokalemia in patients with good renal function, and acidosis. It is contraindicated in hyponatremia.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: De-gloving injury refers to ______
options: Skin and subcutaneous fat are stripped from the underlying fascia
Skin, subcutaneous fat and fascia are stripped from tendons
Skin, subcutaneous fat, fascia and tendons are stripped from bone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Skin and subcutaneous fat are stripped from the underlying fascia

Degloving is the avulsion of skin and subcutaneous fat from the underlying fascia, muscle or bone.

Degloving injuries can be open or closed. An example of open degloving injury is finger avulsion injury with loss of skin. Closed degloving injuries result from shearing forces (e.g. motor vehicle collisions).

The extent of degloving injuries are often underappreciated and much of the skin may be non-viable.  Disruption of perforating vascular and lymphatic vessels may result in a characteristic haemolymphatic collection between the fascial planes called a Morel-Lavallée lesion.

Patterns of degloving injury:

1. Limited degloving with abrasion or avulsion
2. Non-circumferential degloving
3. Circumferential single plane degloving
4. Circumferential multiplanar degloving

Assessing the viability of degloved tissue can be difficult and may therefore require more than one surgical exploration and debridement before definitive reconstruction. Non-viable skin may show fixed staining and thrombosis of subcutaneous veins. Most surgeons serially excise the degloved skin until punctate dermal bleeding is seen from viable tissue.

Intravenous fluorescein can help in delineating non-viable tissue, but it requires specialist equipment and there is a small risk of anaphylaxis. Indocyanine green has been found to have less risk of allergy.

Open degloving injuries are managed by reattaching the viable skin and grafting. Closed degloving injuries are managed by draining the accumulated fluid, removing the dead tissue and sclerotherapy. For severe, multiplanar degloving, amputation is done.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What will be the diagnosis of the image given below:
questions.explanation: The image shows multiple round viral particles with a dense central core and surrounding capsid, arranged in a clustered pattern within a host cell. This morphology is characteristic of the Herpes simplex virus (HSV) on electron microscopy. HSV is a large, enveloped DNA virus with an icosahedral capsid and a distinct electron-dense core, often seen in groups within infected cells. The presence of uniform spherical particles with clear capsid outlines and internal density helps distinguish HSV from other viruses. Why Other Options Are Wrong (A) HIV: Appears pleomorphic with a conical core, not uniform icosahedral particles. (B) Hepatitis B virus: Shows Dane particles with smaller spherical and filamentous forms, not clustered capsids like this. (C) Human papillomavirus: Non-enveloped virus with different capsid appearance and not typically seen in such clustered intracellular EM patterns

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young patient presents with unexplained hair loss and persistent abdominal discomfort. During surgery, a mass is retrieved from the stomach (as shown in the image). What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of unexplained hair loss (alopecia due to trichotillomania) and persistent abdominal discomfort in a young patient is highly suggestive of a Trichobezoar. A bezoar is a mass of trapped, undigested material in the stomach, and a trichobezoar is specifically composed of ingested hair. Over time, the hair forms a large, solid cast that takes the shape of the entire stomach, as shown in the provided surgical image. Splenic rupture (Option B) presents with acute hemoperitoneum and shock. Pancreatic necrosis (Option C) is a complication of severe acute pancreatitis. Carcinoma of the stomach (Option D) is rare in young patients and does not explain the alopecia. A large trichobezoar that extends into the small intestine is known as "Rapunzel syndrome." Diagnosis is often made via ultrasound or endoscopy. Management typically requires surgical removal via gastrotomy, as these masses are usually too large and dense for endoscopic retrieval. Psychiatric referral for the underlying hair-pulling and eating behaviors is essential to prevent recurrence
questions.learning: The clinical combination of unexplained hair loss (alopecia due to trichotillomania) and persistent abdominal discomfort in a young patient is highly suggestive of a Trichobezoar.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented with jaw swelling and weight loss. Suspecting a malignancy, the submandibular gland was resected. Which is the most likely nerve to be damaged during submandibular gland resection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lingual nerve

The most likely nerve to be damaged during submandibular gland resection is the lingual nerve.

It loops around the submandibular duct and hence is susceptible to injury during submandibular gland resection.

Course:

The lingual nerve arises from the posterior trunk of the mandibular nerve (V3 branch of the trigeminal nerve). The lingual nerve descends between the tensor veli palatini muscle and the lateral pterygoid muscle, where it is joined by the chorda tympani nerve. It then descends across the medial pterygoid muscle to enter the oral cavity. As the lingual nerve enters the floor of the oral cavity, it lies on the deep portion of the submandibular gland. It then passes into the tongue on the hyoglossus muscle where it is attached to the submandibular ganglion.

The submandibular duct lies between the lingual and hypoglossal nerves, superficial to the hyoglossus muscle. As the duct reaches the anterior border of the hyoglossus, it is crossed by the lingual nerve and lies in close proximity to the nerve. Hence lingual nerve injury is the most common.

Injury:

The lingual nerve is at risk to be injured during submandibular gland resection because dissection of the submandibular duct from the nerve is required. Also, it is connected to the submandibular ganglion which will lead to the nerve being exposed within the operating field.

The manifestations of lingual nerve injury depend on whether the lesion is proximal or distal to where it is joined by the chorda tympani nerve.

• Proximal injury: There is loss of sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, gingivae, oral mucosa, lower lip, and chin.
• Distal injury: In addition to features of proximal injury, secretion from the salivary glands below the oral fissure and taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is also lost.

Note:

The cranial nerves that are at risk during submandibular gland resection include:

• The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve
• Lingual nerve
• Hypoglossal nerve

Other options:

Option A: Nerve to mylohyoid is a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve and lies in the mylohyoid groove inferior to the mandibular foramen, hence the risk of injury is less.

Option B: Inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandibular canal via the mandibular foramen, hence is unlikely to be injured during submandibular gland excision.

Option D: Hypoglossal nerve injury is less common than lingual nerve injury as it only lies below and parallels to the submandibular duct.
questions.learning: Lingual nerve — The most likely nerve to be damaged during submandibular gland resection is the lingual nerve. It loops around the submandibular duct and hence is susceptible to injury during submandibular gland resection.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 60-year-old individual presents with an ulcer near the medial canthus of the eye. The lesion has rolled-out, beaded margins. Histopathological examination reveals nests of cells showing peripheral palisading. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical description of an ulcer with rolled-out, beaded margins located at the medial canthus is a classic presentation of Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC), the most common skin cancer. The diagnosis is confirmed by histopathology, which characteristically shows nesting of basaloid cells with a distinctive peripheral palisading pattern of nuclei. Regarding the distractors, Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Option A) typically presents with a scaly or keratinized appearance and lacks the pearly, beaded margins. A nevus (Option B) is a benign lesion and would not show these malignant histological features. Melanoma (Option D) usually presents as an irregularly pigmented macule or nodule rather than a slow-growing ulcer with palisading cells. BCC is slow-growing and rarely metastasizes but can be locally invasive. Therefore, the combination of clinical margins and palisading histology
questions.learning: The clinical description of an ulcer with rolled-out, beaded margins located at the medial canthus is a classic presentation of Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC), the most common skin cancer.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding the staffing pattern of an Urban Primary Health Centre (UPHC) is incorrect?
questions.explanation: Under the Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) guidelines, the staffing pattern for an Urban Primary Health Center (U-PHC) is specifically defined. A standard U-PHC is staffed by 4 to 5 staff nurses in total. Statement B is often considered "false" in examinations because the specific core staffing recommendation for a U-PHC typically lists 2 staff nurses as the essential baseline requirement for a facility serving a 50,000 population, with additional staff depending on the workload. The center does include 2 doctors (Option A—usually 1 full-time and 1 part-time/regular), 1 lab technician (Option C), and 1 pharmacist (Option D). The U-PHC serves as the primary urban healthcare delivery point, focusing on outpatient services and outreach. Therefore, according to fixed standard staffing charts, the figure of 5 multi-skilled nurses is an overstatement of the essential baseline staff

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 65-year-old man undergoing evaluation for suspected renal dysfunction has his creatinine clearance measured. Which statement best describes the significance and interpretation of creatinine clearance?
questions.explanation: Creatinine clearance is a widely used clinical measure to estimate the Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR). It is considered comparable to inulin clearance, which is the "gold standard" for measuring GFR. Inulin is perfect because it is freely filtered but neither reabsorbed nor secreted. Creatinine is also freely filtered and not reabsorbed; however, a small amount is actively secreted by the renal tubules. This secretion causes creatinine clearance to slightly overestimate the true GFR (by about 10-20%). Despite this, it is far more practical for clinical use than inulin, which requires a continuous infusion. It is not "superior" (Option C) in accuracy, nor "inferior" (Option B) in clinical utility. It is not identical to renal plasma flow (Option D), which is much higher. For most clinical purposes, creatinine clearance provides a sufficiently accurate estimate of kidney function. Consequently, it remains the standard-of-care proxy for GFR in everyday medical practice
questions.learning: Creatinine clearance is a widely used clinical measure to estimate the Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR). It is considered comparable to inulin clearance, which is the "gold standard" for measuring GFR.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Identify the cell marked in the histological image of the cerebellum shown below
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Purkinje cell

The structure marked in the image is a flask-shaped neuron in the cerebellar cortex, which is a Purkinje cell.

Purkinje cells are the flask-shaped cells present in the Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum. They are evenly spaced and arranged in a single layer between molecular and granular cell layers. The dendrite from each cell passes upward to enter the molecular layer and the axon of each cell passes downwards, crosses the granular cell layer, and terminates on the deep cerebellar nuclei. They are inhibitory and use GABA as their neurotransmitter.

Axons of Purkinje cells are the only efferents of the cerebellar cortex. They receive excitatory input from the climbing fibers from the inferior olivary nucleus and mossy fibers.

Pathological significance of Purkinje cells:

* Negri bodies in rabies are usually found as eosinophilic, cytoplasmic inclusions in the neurons of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum.

* In paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, there is the destruction of Purkinje cells due to antibodies directed against them.

* Purkinje cells and neurons in pyramidal cell layers of the hippocampus and cerebral cortex are the most sensitive neurons to hypoxia and are likely to be damaged in cases of global cerebral ischemia.

Pearl PF2096: Layers of the cerebellar cortex

The cerebellar cortex is divided into 3 layers. They are:

* Molecular layer - It is the outermost layer. It contains stellate cells and basket cells. They receive excitatory input from the parallel fibers and form inhibitory synapses on the Purkinje cells. It contains many myelinated and unmyelinated nerve fibers giving it a pale appearance in H and E staining.

* Purkinje layer - It is the middle layer. It contain flask-shaped cell bodies of Purkinje cells. Their dendrites pass into the molecular layer. The axons of the Purkinje cells passes through the granular layer into the white matter and synapses with the cerebellar nuclei.

* Granular layer - It is the innermost layer. It contains the cell bodies of the granule cells as well as Golgi cells. It receives excitatory input from the mossy fibers. They end on the dendrites of the granule cells and these complexes are called glomeruli. The axon from the granule cells travels to the molecular layer and bifurcates in a T-shape. These branches form the T and are called parallel fibers. These parallel fibers form excitatory synapses with the Purkinje cells. The granule cells form the only excitatory neurons in the cerebellar cortex. Golgi cells receive input from parallel fibers and mossy fibers. They send inhibitory output to the granule cells.

Neurotransmitters released:

* Stellate, basket, Golgi and Purkinje cells- GABA

* Granule cells - Glutamate

The only output from the cerebellar cortex is inhibitory from the Purkinje cells to the deep cerebellar nuclei.
questions.learning: Purkinje cell — The structure marked in the image is a flask-shaped neuron in the cerebellar cortex, which is a Purkinje cell. Purkinje cells are the flask-shaped cells present in the Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-year-old girl presents with markedly unequal visual acuity between her eyes (right eye 20/60, left eye 20/20), while her eye examination, including the fundus, is otherwise normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Amblyopia, commonly known as "lazy eye," is a developmental disorder where the brain fails to process inputs from one eye, favoring the other. The hallmark of amblyopia is a significant difference in visual acuity between the two eyes (anisometropia) in the setting of a physically normal eye examination. Because the fundus exam and external structures are normal, primary pathologies like Retinoblastoma (Option B, which causes leukocoria) or Congenital Cataracts (Option C, which shows a cloudy lens) are ruled out. A brain lesion (Option A) would typically cause visual field defects or other neurological signs rather than isolated reduced acuity in one eye. Amblyopia occurs because the visual cortex does not develop properly during the "critical period" of childhood when the brain receives blurred or suppressed images from the affected eye. Therefore, given the age and the "normal" structural exam, amblyopia is the definitive diagnosis. Treatment involves patching the stronger eye to force the brain to use the weaker one

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient presents to the hospital claiming to be experiencing a cardiac arrest. After a thorough medical evaluation, he is found to be physically healthy but refuses to leave the hospital. He reports a recent history of being held at gunpoint during a robbery. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with acute psychological distress following a life-threatening traumatic event (being held at gunpoint). His irrational belief of having a "cardiac arrest" and refusal to leave the hospital are manifestations of the intense anxiety and hyperarousal seen in Acute Stress Disorder (ASD). ASD is diagnosed when symptoms occur within one month of the trauma. If symptoms persist beyond one month, the diagnosis changes to Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). Schizophrenia (Option B) is characterized by chronic hallucinations and delusions unrelated to a specific acute trauma. Avoidant personality disorder (Option C) is a long-term pattern of social inhibition. Delirium (Option D) involves an acute, fluctuating change in consciousness due to a medical cause. Management of ASD involves psychological first aid, trauma-focused therapy, and occasionally short-term benzodiazepines. The acute, trauma-linked nature of the symptoms is the key to this diagnosis

questions.text:
A patient following a skid resulting in a motor traffic accident was brought to the emergency room 2 hours later. On examination, he was stable with GCS 15/15. The pupil was reactive to light. Tenderness and bruising over the left lower chest wall with petechiae was seen. Severe tenderness was elicited in the left hypochondriac region and BP- 90/50 mm of Hg. What is the best investigation used in the ER?

GCS- Glasgow coma scale

FAST- Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. FAST

FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma) is the best investigation that can be performed in the emergency room (ER) for this patient with a blood pressure of 90/50 mm Hg who has sustained blunt abdominal trauma.

Focussed assessment with sonography for trauma is a non-invasive investigation that can be performed rapidly in the emergency room. It helps in identifying an abnormal collection of fluid or blood. FAST is indicated in:

• Haemodynamically unstable patients who had a blunt abdominal trauma
• Patients who sustained penetrating abdominal trauma with no other indications for immediate laparotomy (signs of haemodynamic instability, peritoneal irritation, peritoneal penetration and gunshot wound with transperitoneal trajectory).

FAST includes an examination of four regions:

• Pericardial sac
• Hepatorenal fossa
• Splenorenal fossa, and
• Pouch of Douglas

It is an operator-dependent procedure with limited visualization of the retroperitoneal structures.

Other options:

Option B - A chest X-Ray is used to exclude hemothorax or pneumothorax in a hemodynamically normal patient with penetrating trauma above the umbilicus or a suspected thoracoabdominal injury. Since the given patient is alert, awake, and with no mention of any pelvic pain or tenderness, a pelvic X-Ray is not indicated either.

Option C - Diagnostic peritoneal lavage is an invasive procedure and requires surgical expertise. For these reasons, it is done only in centres where FAST and/ CT are not available.

Option D - CT scan requires transporting the patient and is time-consuming. Hence, it cannot be performed in the ER in a haemodynamically unstable patient.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman at 30 weeks presents with painful bleeding PV, reduced fetal movement, increased uterine tone, and absent FHR. BP is 166/98 mmHg, and the cervix is 6 cm dilated, 70% effaced with intact membranes. What is the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Start Antihypertensives and ARM

These findings are typical of Placental Abruption with intrauterine fetal demise (IUFD). Placental abruption occurs when the placenta separates prematurely from the uterine wall, causing bleeding behind the placenta.

Classic features

| Feature | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Painful bleeding PV | Placental separation

| Hypertonic uterus | Blood irritates myometrium

| Fetal distress or death | Reduced placental perfusion

| Hypertension | Major risk factor

The fetus in this case has already died (absent FHR).

Therefore the goal is rapid vaginal delivery to protect the mother. Artificial rupture of membranes (ARM) helps by:

• Reducing uterine pressure
• Accelerating labour
• Controlling bleeding

A) Emergency LSCS

Cesarean section is indicated only if fetus is alive.

B) Antihypertensives + LSCS

Again unnecessary because IUFD already occurred.

D) Tocolysis

Tocolytics suppress labour and are contraindicated in placental abruption.
questions.learning: Start Antihypertensives and ARM — These findings are typical of Placental Abruption with intrauterine fetal demise (IUFD). Placental abruption occurs when the placenta separates prematurely from the uterine wall, causing bleeding behind the placenta.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following amino acids, which is categorized as a nonessential amino acid?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Proline

Amino acids are classified as essential and nonessential based on whether they can be synthesized by the human body.

• Essential amino acids must be obtained from the diet.
• Nonessential amino acids can be synthesized in sufficient amounts by the body.

Proline is a nonessential amino acid because it is synthesized from glutamate in the body. It is important for collagen synthesis and wound healing.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Leucine: Essential, branched-chain amino acid (BCAA).
• B. Threonine: Essential amino acid.
• C. Tryptophan: Essential amino acid; precursor of serotonin, melatonin, and niacin (vitamin B3).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman presents with acute onset abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She has a low-grade fever, with a pulse rate of 90 bpm and blood pressure of 126/84 mm Hg. She has regular menstrual cycles of 28 days. Pelvic examination shows a tender right adnexal mass. Ovarian torsion is suspected. What is the investigation of choice in this condition? Urine pregnancy testing- negative Serum β-HCG level- 1 mIU/L
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Doppler Ultrasound

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of ovarian torsion. The investigation of choice for an ovarian torsion is a doppler sonography.

Torsion of the ovaries is a gynecological emergency and is most commonly seen in women of the reproductive age group. Ovarian cysts including mucous cystadenomas and dermoid cysts have the highest risks of undergoing torsion. Adnexal masses measuring >6 cm in diameter have the highest rates of torsion.

A patient with torsion presents with sharp lower abdominal pain, usually localized to the involved side with radiation to the flank, groin, or thigh. Nausea and vomiting are commonly associated. Adnexal necrosis may cause a low-grade fever.

During torsion, the low-pressure veins are initially compressed by the twisting pedicle. This leads to continuous inflow with decreased outflow causing stromal edema and congestion. The increasing stromal swelling later compresses the arteries causing ischemia and necrosis.

On a doppler USG, the ovary appears enlarged, globular, and has a heterogenous appearance compared to the contralateral ovary due to edema, engorgement, and hemorrhage. Twisting of the vascular pedicle may give rise to a 'whirlpool sign', a round hyperechoic structure with concentric hypoechoic stripes. MRI or CT imaging can be used in patients with normal Doppler but with characteristic signs and symptoms of torsion, to confirm or rule out the diagnosis.

Management involves urgent laparotomy or laparoscopic evaluation. Salvage of the involved adnexa with the removal of any associated cyst/tumor and possible oophoropexy are the goals. However, necrosis of the adnexa necessitates the removal of the adnexal structures.
questions.learning: Doppler Ultrasound — The above clinical scenario is suggestive of ovarian torsion. The investigation of choice for an ovarian torsion is a doppler sonography.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: As a neuron's diameter increases, what effect manifests?
questions.explanation: The diameter of an axon is a major determinant of how rapidly an action potential can travel. A larger axonal diameter results in a significantly lower internal (axial) resistance to current flow. This reduced resistance allows local electrical currents to spread more efficiently and quickly along the interior of the axon, enabling faster depolarization of the adjacent membrane segments. Consequently, larger neurons exhibit a higher conduction velocity. This principle is vital in motor neurons where high-speed signal transmission is required. Option B is incorrect as velocity increases with size. Membrane resistance (Option C) per unit length actually decreases with larger surface areas, but the reduction in axial resistance dominates the change in speed. Action potential amplitude (Option D) is determined by ionic equilibrium potentials rather than physical axon size. Thus, diameter and speed are directly proportional
questions.learning: The diameter of an axon is a major determinant of how rapidly an action potential can travel. A larger axonal diameter results in a significantly lower internal (axial) resistance to current flow.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Immediately after childbirth, assessment of uterine position is important for postpartum care. What is the normal position of the uterus immediately following delivery?
questions.explanation: After the third stage of labor (delivery of the placenta), the uterus undergoes immediate contraction to prevent postpartum hemorrhage. This physiological process, known as involution, causes the fundus to become firm and globoid. Immediately after delivery, the fundus of the uterus is typically felt at a level roughly midway between the pubic symphysis and the umbilicus, which is below the umbilicus (Option C). Within a few hours, the uterus may rise slightly to the level of the umbilicus due to the relaxation of pelvic floor muscles and bladder filling. Option A (below pubic symphysis) is incorrect as the uterus only returns to its true pelvic, non-palpable position around 2 weeks postpartum. Option D (above umbilicus) is often an abnormal finding, potentially suggesting a full bladder or uterine atony with retained blood. Monitoring this "below the umbilicus" position is standard for ensuring uterine contraction
questions.learning: After the third stage of labor (delivery of the placenta), the uterus undergoes immediate contraction to prevent postpartum hemorrhage. This physiological process, known as involution, causes the fundus to become firm and globoid.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What is the poisoning associated with increased gastrointestinal secretions and diarrhea?
options: Organophosphates [not listed in options, but contextually relevant]
questions.explanation: Organophosphates. [contextual correction] (Note: The options provided in the source—Cocaine, Crack, Cannabis, Ketamine—all typically cause sympathergic or anticholinergic effects like constipation or dry mouth. Diarrhea is a classic cholinergic symptom.) A poisoning characterized by increased gastrointestinal secretions and diarrhea is most classically associated with Organophosphate (OP) compounds. These agents inhibit acetylcholinesterase, leading to a "cholinergic crisis." The hallmark symptoms are remembered by the mnemonic SLUDGE: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urinary incontinence, Diarrhea, Gastrointestinal cramps, and Emesis. Cocaine (Option A) and Crack (Option B) are sympathomimetics that cause tachycardia and hypertension. Cannabis (Option C) often causes reddening of the eyes and increased appetite. Ketamine (Option D) is a dissociative anesthetic. OP poisoning is a medical emergency requiring the use of Atropine to block the excess muscarinic activity and Pralidoxime (PAM) to reactivate the enzyme. Correct identification of these toxidromes is essential for initiating life-saving antidotal therapy.
questions.learning: Organophosphates. [contextual correction] (Note: The options provided in the source—Cocaine, Crack, Cannabis, Ketamine—all typically cause sympathergic or anticholinergic effects like constipation or dry mouth.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following stains is used for the detection of hemosiderin deposits?
questions.explanation: Hemosiderin is an iron-storage complex composed of ferritin and other materials. In pathology, detecting hemosiderin is critical for diagnosing conditions like hemochromatosis or identifying old areas of hemorrhage. Perl's Prussian blue is the specific histochemical stain used for this purpose. It reacts with the ferric iron in hemosiderin to produce a bright blue color. Mason-Fontana stain (Option A) is used to detect melanin. Oil red O (Option B) and Sudan black (Option C) are specialized stains for lipids and fats. Since the other options target different biological molecules, Perl's Prussian blue remains the definitive method for visualizing iron deposits in tissue sections. This stain is widely used in liver, bone marrow, and lung biopsies to identify various pathological processes involving iron accumulation
questions.learning: Hemosiderin is an iron-storage complex composed of ferritin and other materials. In pathology, detecting hemosiderin is critical for diagnosing conditions like hemochromatosis or identifying old areas of hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Considering the disease depicted in the given image, which of the following specimens would not be expected to contain filarial worms?
questions.explanation: The image shows elephantiasis, the chronic stage of lymphatic filariasis caused by Wuchereria bancrofti or Brugia malayi. The adult worms live in the lymphatic system, and the female worms release microfilariae into the host's circulation. Microfilariae can be found in the "blood" (Option A), typically showing nocturnal periodicity. They can also be found in "urine" in patients with chyluria (Option C) or in "hydrocele fluid" (Option D), which is a common manifestation in males. Filarial worms are "not found in saliva" (Option B), as there is no anatomical or physiological mechanism for the worms or microfilariae to enter the salivary secretions. Diagnosis is often made by demonstrating microfilariae in a midnight blood smear or by detecting circulating filarial antigens. Elephantiasis results from chronic lymphatic obstruction and secondary fibrosis. Management involves mass drug administration with diethylcarbamazine (DEC) and albendazole, alongside meticulous local skin hygiene to prevent secondary bacterial infections that worsen the limb swelling
questions.learning: The image shows elephantiasis, the chronic stage of lymphatic filariasis caused by Wuchereria bancrofti or Brugia malayi. The adult worms live in the lymphatic system, and the female worms release microfilariae into the host's circulation.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: With respect to tuberculosis of hip, which of the marked areas are affected commonly?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1

The most common area affected is acetabulum which is marked as 1 in the figure.

Multiple cavitations occurs in femoral head and the acetabulum. Eventually, the head or the acetabulum gets partially absorbed. By the constant pull of the muscles acting on the hip, the remaining head of femur may dislocate from the acetabulum onto the ilium,giving rise to the so called wandering acetabulum.

Early stages of tb hip are characterised by synovial hypertrophy and effusion. The pannus of the hypertrophied synovium extends fully around the articular cartilage destroying it. The joint is filled with pus and granulation tissue.

The sequential destruction is:

* Dislocation of femoral head

* Destruction of articular cartilage

* Synovial hypertrophy

* Multiple cavitations

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A female patient presents with nasal obstruction, nasal discharge, and loss of smell. On examination, foul-smelling discharge and yellowish-green crusts are present in the nasal cavity. She is found to have merciful anosmia. Which of the following finding can also be seen during the examination of her nose?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Roomy nasal cavity

The clinical vignette of anosmia, foul-smelling discharge, and yellowish-green crusts in the nasal cavity points to a diagnosis of atrophic rhinitis. The other examination finding that is observed in atrophic rhinitis is a roomy nasal cavity.

Atrophic rhinitis is a chronic inflammation of the nose characterized by atrophy of nasal mucosa and turbinate bones. The exact etiology of this condition is not known.

The patients present with nasal obstruction, foul odor, merciful anosmia, greenish-grey crusting of the nasal passage, pale nasal mucosa, atrophied nasal turbinates, and epistaxis following the removal of the crusts. Roomy nasal cavity is seen due to the resorption of bones of the turbinates.

Treatment options for atrophic rhinitis include nasal irrigation using warm saline or an alkaline solution composed of sodium bicarbonate, sodium biborate, and sodium chloride (1:1:2) mixed with water.

Local antibiotics such as Kemicetine antiozaena solution, which contains chloromycetin, oestradiol, and vitamin D2, can be used. Topical applications of 25% glucose in glycerine, estradiol spray, and systemic administration of streptomycin, potassium iodide, or placental extract may also be employed.

Surgical management options include Young's operation, where flaps are raised within the nasal vestibule and both nostrils are completely closed, then opened after 6 months. During this time, the nasal mucosa may revert to a more normal state, and crusting is reduced. Another option is the modified Young's operation, where the nostrils are partially closed to avoid discomfort. The results of this modified approach are comparable to the original Young's operation.

Additionally, the nasal cavity can be narrowed through submucosal injection of teflon paste or by inserting fat, cartilage, or teflon strips beneath the mucoperiosteum.

The image below shows the endoscopic appearance of atrophic rhinitis:

Other options:

Option B: Nasal polyps are non-neoplastic masses of the edematous nasal or sinus mucosa. Nasal polyps can be antrochoanal polyps or ethmoidal polyps.

Option C: Inferior turbinate hypertrophy is associated with various mucosal diseases which include allergic rhinitis, infectious rhinitis, and vasomotor rhinitis. It can cause chronic nasal obstruction.

Option D: Foreign body nose is commonly seen in children and the child presents with unilateral, foul-smelling nasal discharge.
questions.learning: Roomy nasal cavity — The clinical vignette of anosmia, foul-smelling discharge, and yellowish-green crusts in the nasal cavity points to a diagnosis of atrophic rhinitis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What type of shock is most likely in a patient with profuse bleeding, cold extremities, and a reduced central venous pressure (CVP)?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of "excessive bleeding" (hemorrhage) is the primary cause of acute volume loss, leading to Hypovolemic Shock (Option B). The physiological response to low circulating volume includes intense peripheral vasoconstriction to divert blood to vital organs, resulting in the "cool extremities" observed. Central Venous Pressure (CVP) is a direct measure of the preload and volume status; a "decreased CVP" confirms that the heart is not receiving enough blood to maintain cardiac output. Cardiogenic shock (Option A) would show an increased CVP due to the heart's failure to pump available blood. Obstructive shock (Option C), such as cardiac tamponade, would also present with an elevated CVP. Hypoadrenal shock (Option D) is a distributive type of shock and would not be the primary diagnosis in a patient with active bleeding. Therefore, the combination of blood loss and low filling pressures is diagnostic of hypovolemia. Management requires immediate hemorrhage control and volume replacement

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the obstetric grip being depicted in the image?
questions.explanation: The image depicts the Fourth Leopold manoeuvre, also known as the Pelvic Grip. In this manoeuvre, the clinician faces the mother's feet and places their hands on either side of the lower uterine segment just above the pelvic inlet. Its primary purpose is to determine the degree of fetal head engagement and to identify the fetal "brow" or "occiput" (the cephalic prominence). Fundal grip (Option C, First manoeuvre) involves palpating the upper uterus while facing the mother. Umbilical grip (Option D, Second manoeuvre) involves palpating the fetal back and limbs on either side of the abdomen. The Third manoeuvre (Pawlik's grip) involves a single hand over the symphysis. Hudsons grip (Option B) is not a standard obstetric term. The specific orientation of the clinician facing the feet while assessing the pelvic contents identifies this as the fourth manoeuvre. It is the final step in the clinical assessment of fetal lie and presentation
questions.learning: The image depicts the Fourth Leopold manoeuvre, also known as the Pelvic Grip. In this manoeuvre, the clinician faces the mother's feet and places their hands on either side of the lower uterine segment just above the pelvic inlet.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which pair of neurotransmitters is associated with depression?
questions.explanation: The "monoamine hypothesis" of depression proposes that the condition results from a deficiency of certain neurotransmitters in the brain. The two most critical neurotransmitters involved are Serotonin and Norepinephrine (Option B). Serotonin (5-HT) regulates mood, sleep, and appetite, while norepinephrine (noradrenaline) is involved in energy, focus, and the stress response. Most modern antidepressants work by increasing the synaptic levels of these two chemicals . For example, SSRIs target serotonin, while SNRIs target both. While dopamine (Option C) also plays a role in the brain's reward system and its lack can contribute to anhedonia (loss of pleasure), the most standard pairing taught in medical and psychiatric texts regarding the core pathophysiology of depression is serotonin and norepinephrine. GABA (Option A and D) is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter and is more closely associated with anxiety disorders. Therefore, the "monoamine" pair is the correct answer
questions.learning: The "monoamine hypothesis" of depression proposes that the condition results from a deficiency of certain neurotransmitters in the brain. The two most critical neurotransmitters involved are Serotonin and Norepinephrine (Option B).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient is suspected to have infective endocarditis. What is the correct number of blood culture samples to be collected?
options: 3 sets of culture samples - Each set has one aerobic and one anaerobic
2 sets of culture samples - Each set has one anaerobic and one aerobic
3 sets of culture samples - Each set has two aerobic and one anaerobic
3 sets of culture samples - Each set has 2 anaerobic only
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 3 sets of culture samples - Each set has one aerobic and one anaerobic

According to the Modified Duke 2023 Criteria for infective endocarditis, when a typical organism is suspected, three separate culture sets are required. Each set will have one aerobic (10 ml) and one anaerobic (10 ml).

According to the new Duke’s criteria, there is no specific timing to draw blood for blood culture. IE is said to be positive for typical organism if two or more blood cultures are positive.

Pearl PF1994: Modified Duke's criteria for diagnosis of infective endocarditis

Diagnosis of Infective endocarditis is by Duke's Criteria, which requires either:

* Pathologic criteria

* Clinical criteria

If clinical criteria are used, definitive endocarditis is defined by the presence of 2 major or 1 major + 3 minor or 5 minor criteria.

The presence of single pathological criteria is definitive of infective endocarditis.

Note: The diagnosis of endocarditis is rejected if an alternative diagnosis is established either when:

* Symptoms resolve and do not recur with <4 days of antibiotic therapy OR

* If surgery or autopsy yields no pathologic or macroscopic evidence of endocarditis in <4 days of antimicrobial therapy.
questions.learning: 3 sets of culture samples - Each set has one aerobic and one anaerobic According to the Modified Duke 2023 Criteria for infective endocarditis, when a typical organism is suspected, three separate culture sets are required.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following amino acids can form oxaloacetate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aspartate

The amino acid Aspartate can be converted into oxaloacetate through a series of enzymatic reactions.

Oxaloacetate is an intermediate in the citric acid cycle (also known as the Krebs cycle or TCA cycle), a key metabolic pathway in cells that generates energy through the oxidation of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins.

Aspartate can be transaminated (an amino group transferred) to form oxaloacetate, which plays a crucial role in linking various metabolic pathways, including the citric acid cycle and gluconeogenesis (the synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources).

Anaplerotic process is the replenishment of the intermediates of the citric acid (Krebs) cycle to replace the catalytic processes and to ensure the continuation of the cycle.

Transamination of aspartate to form oxaloacetate is one of these reactions.

Other anaplerotic reactions:

* Carboxylation of pyruvate to oxaloacetate, which is catalyzed by pyruvate carboxylase.

* Glutamate and glutamine to α-ketoglutarate, a reaction catalyzed by glutamate dehydrogenase and glutaminase, respectively

* Compounds that produce propionyl CoA can be then carboxylated and isomerized to succinyl CoA.

* Pyruvate can be carboxylated to malate.

questions.text: A woman is set to undergo a complete laparoscopic hysterectomy. She wants to know if there are any disadvantages to this procedure. What are the disadvantages of laparoscopic over open surgery?
options: Not knowing the extent of thermal burns
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Not knowing the extent of thermal burns

The disadvantage of laparoscopic over open surgery is not knowing the extent of the thermal burns.

Diathermy burns are a particular hazard in laparoscopic surgery due to the following reasons:

• Relative lack of visibility of the entire instrument.
• Faulty insulation of laparoscopic instruments
• Intraperitoneal contact of the diathermy with another metal instrument while activating the pedal.
• Inadvertent activation of the pedal while the diathermy tip is out of the vision of the camera.
• Retained heat in the diathermy tip touching susceptible structures, such as the bowel.

The advantages of laparoscopic over open surgery are as follows:

• Less postoperative pain (Option D)
• Less blood loss (Option C)
• Cosmetically better
• Earlier recovery and shorter postoperative stay at the hospital (Option A)
• Fewer intraoperative adhesions
• Better perception of anatomy intraoperatively

questions.text: A 60-year-old woman presents with weakness in right arm for 6 hours duration. The weakness gradually became lesser and resolves. She is a known case of diabetes and hypertension and is obese.Which of the following is the probable diagnosis of this case?
