questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text:
Arrange the following in the correct order of symptomatology seen in iron toxicity:

1. Pyloric stricture
2. Asymptomatic phase
3. Gastrointestinal bleeding
4. Liver failure and hypoglycemia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3 -> 2 -> 4 -> 1

The correct order of symptomatology in iron toxicity is 3 -> 2 -> 4 ->1.

Symptoms of iron toxicity are divided into 4 stages:

• Stage 1 (few hours after ingestion): vomiting, abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, shock, acidosis, and coma
• Stage 2 (6-24 hours): Asymptomatic phase
• Stage 3 (24-48 hours): Metabolic acidosis, jaundice, hypoglycemia, shock, coma with hepatic and renal failure.
• Stage 4 (1-2 weeks): Late complications such as gastric stricture and pyloric stenosis.

Iron exerts its toxic effects by increasing capillary permeability, release of hydrogen ions, inhibition of mitochondrial function, and direct corrosive action on the gastric mucosa. Ingestion of 20 to 30 grams is considered to be fatal and the fatal period is around 24-30 hours. Desferrioxamine is the mainstay of treatment with supportive gastric lavage, administration of egg and milk to form iron-protein complexes, oral MgOH solution, and hemodialysis in severe cases.

Postmortem changes in iron toxicity include:

• Hemorrhagic necrosis of gastric mucosa with perforation of gastric or jejunal wall
• Acute hepatic necrosis
• Degenerative renal tubular changes

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the nuclear family life cycle, which stage begins when the family has its first child?
questions.explanation: The developmental cycle of a nuclear family consists of several predictable stages. The stage of Extension (Option A) begins with the birth of the first child . This phase is characterized by the expansion of the family size and the increasing responsibilities of child-rearing. Complete extension (Option B) refers to the point when the family has reached its maximum size (all children are born). The phase of Contraction (Option C) begins when the first child leaves home (often for work or marriage), and the family starts to shrink. Completed contraction (Option D) occurs when all children have left, and the original couple is alone again (the "empty nest" stage). Therefore, because the family is just beginning to grow with its first new member, they are entering the phase of Extension
questions.learning: The developmental cycle of a nuclear family consists of several predictable stages. The stage of Extension (Option A) begins with the birth of the first child .

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presented with unilateral proptosis and bilateral abducent palsy. What is the most probable cause ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cavernous sinus thrombosis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of cavernous sinus thrombosis.

Features of cavernous sinus thrombosis include early involvement lateral rectus palsy (abducent nerve involvement) since it runs through the cavernous sinus. Oculomotor and trochlear nerve palsy occur later as they are related to the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus. Other signs are proptosis, severe supraorbital pain, edema in the mastoid region, absence of corneal sensation, and dilated pupil.

Options A- Retinoblastoma occurs in young children and presents with unilateral proptosis with leukocoria, buphthalmos, and squint.

Option B- Orbital pseudotumor presents with unilateral proptosis with diplopia, conjunctival chemosis. The inflammation is responsive to systemic corticosteroids.

Option C- Orbital cellulitis presents with unilateral proptosis with pain and decreased ocular motility.
questions.learning: Cavernous sinus thrombosis — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of cavernous sinus thrombosis. Features of cavernous sinus thrombosis include early involvement lateral rectus palsy (abducent nerve involvement) since it runs through the cavernous sinus.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study was done to investigate whether three new antibiotics used for urinary tract infections cured the disease or not. Which of the following statistical tests can be used to test the significance of this study?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chi-square test

The outcome in this study is whether urinary tract infection was “cured” or “not cured,” which is a categorical variable.

Since the study compares categorical outcomes among multiple antibiotic groups, the appropriate statistical test is Chi-square test. Chi-square test evaluates association/difference between categorical variables.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Student’s t-test → compares means between 2 groups for continuous data

• Paired t-test → compares paired continuous observations

• ANOVA → compares means among ≥3 groups for continuous variables

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What type of pregnancy is identified on scenographic examination in a 26-year-old woman with 12 weeks of amenorrhea?
questions.explanation: The ultrasound image displays a twin pregnancy with two separate gestational sacs and a characteristically thick dividing membrane. The presence of the "Lambda sign" (or Twin-peak sign), where the membrane meets the placental surface in a triangular shape, is pathognomonic for Dichorionic Diamniotic (DCDA) twins (Option B). This indicates each twin has its own placenta and amniotic sac. Monochorionic diamniotic twins (Option A) share a placenta and would show a thin membrane meeting the placenta in a "T-sign". Monochorionic monoamniotic twins (Option C) share a single sac with no dividing membrane. Conjoined twins (Option D) would show physical fusion of the fetal bodies. Identifying chorionicity at 12 weeks is critical for risk stratification, as monochorionic pregnancies have much higher rates of complications like Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome. Therefore, the thick membrane and lambda sign identify this as a DCDA gestation
questions.learning: The ultrasound image displays a twin pregnancy with two separate gestational sacs and a characteristically thick dividing membrane. The presence of the "Lambda sign" (or Twin-peak sign), where the membrane meets the placental surface in a triangular shape,…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with sudden-onset right-sided hemiparesis. His blood pressure is 200/100 mmHg, and NCCT of the head shows intracerebral hemorrhage. Which of the following interventions should NOT be performed in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation: In any patient presenting with sudden hemiparesis where a Non-Contrast CT (NCCT) has confirmed a brain bleed (intracerebral hemorrhage), Thrombolysis is absolutely contraindicated. Thrombolytic agents like alteplase are only used for ischemic strokes; administering them during a hemorrhage would catastrophically worsen the bleeding. Blood pressure control (Option B) is essential to prevent hematoma expansion, typically targeting a systolic pressure around 140 mmHg. Edema management (Option C), using osmotic agents like mannitol, is necessary if there are signs of increased intracranial pressure. Elective hyperventilation (Option D) may be used briefly as a temporary measure to lower intracranial pressure by causing cerebral vasoconstriction if the patient deteriorates. The management of hemorrhagic stroke focuses on stabilization, neurosurgical consultation if indicated, and intensive monitoring to prevent secondary brain injury. Differentiating between ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke via imaging is the most critical first step in the entire stroke management algorithm
questions.learning: In any patient presenting with sudden hemiparesis where a Non-Contrast CT (NCCT) has confirmed a brain bleed (intracerebral hemorrhage), Thrombolysis is absolutely contraindicated.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 4-year- old boy presenting with a red rash on the cheeks that spreads to the trunk and limbs, accompanied by low-grade fever, headache, and mild upper respiratory symptoms, caused by a single-stranded DNA virus?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a "slapped-cheek" red rash followed by a generalized spread is the classic description of Erythema Infectiosum (also known as Fifth Disease). This condition is caused by Parvovirus B19. The question provides a definitive virological clue: the causative organism is a single-stranded DNA virus, which is the unique genomic classification of Parvoviruses. Scarlet fever (Option A) is caused by bacteria and presents with a "sandpaper" rash and strawberry tongue. Exanthema subitum (Option C), or Roseola, is caused by HHV-6 (double-stranded DNA) and features a high fever followed by a rash after the fever drops. Rubeola (Option D), or Measles, is an RNA virus presenting with Koplik spots and a more severe prodrome. Therefore, the specific genomic type and pathognomonic cheek rash confirm Erythema Infectiosum
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a "slapped-cheek" red rash followed by a generalized spread is the classic description of Erythema Infectiosum (also known as Fifth Disease).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the eye manifestation seen in HLA B27- positive patients with ulcerative colitis?
questions.explanation: Patients with HLA-B27-positive inflammatory bowel disease, such as ulcerative colitis, have a significantly increased risk for extraintestinal autoimmune manifestations. The most classic ocular complication is acute anterior uveitis. It typically presents with sudden eye pain, redness (ciliary flush), photophobia, and blurred vision. Conjunctivitis (Option B) is more common in reactive arthritis and involves a more superficial inflammation. Scleritis (Option C) presents with deep, boring pain and is more often linked to systemic diseases like rheumatoid arthritis. While iridocyclitis (Option D) is a subset of anterior uveitis, the general and clinically preferred term for this broad extraintestinal manifestation in IBD is uveitis. Therefore, uveitis is the standard diagnostic answer for this autoimmune link
questions.learning: Patients with HLA-B27-positive inflammatory bowel disease, such as ulcerative colitis, have a significantly increased risk for extraintestinal autoimmune manifestations.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What electrolyte disturbance is most commonly associated with this postoperative condition, as demonstrated in the provided X-ray image?
questions.explanation: The erect abdominal X-ray (Option R) shows multiple dilated loops of small and large bowel with air throughout, which is characteristic of a paralytic ileus. This condition involves the temporary cessation of intestinal peristalsis, frequently occurring after abdominal surgery. Hypokalemia (low serum potassium) (Option B) is the most common electrolyte imbalance that directly causes or worsens a paralytic ileus. Potassium is essential for the normal electrical activity and contraction of intestinal smooth muscle; its deficiency leads to gut atony. Options A, C, and D (Hypocalcemia, Hyperkalemia, and Hypercalcemia) are less classically associated with the development of postoperative gut paralysis . Management involves "drip and suck" (nasogastric decompression and IV fluids) and, crucially, the correction of the underlying electrolyte deficits. Once potassium levels are normalized, peristalsis usually returns spontaneously. Therefore, monitoring potassium is a vital part of postoperative care
questions.learning: The erect abdominal X-ray (Option R) shows multiple dilated loops of small and large bowel with air throughout, which is characteristic of a paralytic ileus.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy with sensorineural hearing loss and eye defects presents to the OPD with hematuria. His renal biopsy on light microscopy was normal. Family history reveals the maternal uncle had Gr 5 CKD an is undergoing dialysis. Which of the following would be the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Alport syndrome

The clinical presentation of a child with hematuria, sensorineural hearing loss, and eye defects with normal renal biopsy is consistent with Alport Syndrome. It is a hereditary nephritis, which explains the family history of chronic kidney disease.

Alport syndrome is a genetic disease caused by mutations in the COL4A5 gene, which codes for the alpha chain of type IV collagen. In approximately 85% of cases, the syndrome is X-linked.

In the early years (around 5 years), patients are often asymptomatic but may have persistent microscopic hematuria. Between 5 and 10 years of age, proteinuria, and hypertension may develop, which can be managed with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors. By 10 years of age, serum creatinine levels start to rise. Around 15 years, patients may experience ear, nose, and throat (ENT) manifestations, with high-frequency sensory neural hearing loss being a common feature in males. Ocular manifestations, such as anterior lenticonus (pathognomonic) and dot and fleck retinopathy (most common), typically appear around the age of 20. Anterior lenticonus is particularly correlated with the development of end-stage renal disease (ESRD). By 25 to 30 years of age, most individuals with Alport's syndrome progress to ESRD.

Gross hematuria following upper respiratory tract infections is not typically seen in Alport's syndrome and should prompt consideration of other conditions, such as IgA nephropathy.

Skin immunofluorescence to demonstrate the lack of the α5(IV) collagen chain and genetic testing can be used for the diagnosis. Light microscopy and immunofluorescence (IF) on renal biopsy may be normal. Electron microscopy reveals irregular areas of thinning and thickening of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), along with splitting of the lamina densa, giving it a basket-weave appearance.

The mainstay of management is the control of hypertension and ACE inhibitors to slow down the progression of renal damage. Although transplant recipients develop anti-GBM antibodies, graft survival is good.

Thin GBM disease is an autosomal dominant disease characterized by persistent microscopic hematuria but no progression to ESRD or extrarenal manifestations. EM can be used to confirm the diagnosis, showing GBM thickness of less than 200 nm.

Other options:

Option B: Goodpasture syndrome is an immune-mediated disease with antibodies against the alpha-3 chain of GBM type IV collagen; it is not hereditary and the light microscopy would reveal extra capillary proliferation with crescents & necrosis.

Option C: In IgA Nephropathy, light microscopy would reveal focal mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis & mesangial widening.

Option D:  In post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), there will be diffuse endocapillary proliferation and accompanying leukocytic infiltration seen in light microscopy.
questions.learning: Alport syndrome — The clinical presentation of a child with hematuria, sensorineural hearing loss, and eye defects with normal renal biopsy is consistent with Alport Syndrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 22-year-old male was brought to the ER after sustaining an astride injury. Following the trauma, he experienced an urge to urinate but was unable to pass urine. On examination, blood was present at the urethral meatus. What is likely to be injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bulbar urethra

The given clinical scenario with a history of an astride injury, blood at the tip of the meatus, and inability to pass urine are all suggestive of an injury to the bulbar urethra.

Astride injury refers to trauma that occurs when a person falls with their perineum straddling a hard object, leading to blunt perineal trauma.

Urethral injuries can be classified into:

Type
Proximal urethral injury
Distal urethral injury

Site of injury

• Prostatic urethra
• Membranous urethra

• Bulbar urethra
• Penile urethra

Mechanism
Secondary to pelvic fracture

Occurs due to a blow to the perineum by:

• Straddle injury
• Gymnasium accidents

Clinical features

• Urinary retention
• Blood at the urethral meatus
• High-riding prostate on digital rectal examination (Vermooten sign)
• Deep perineal hematoma

• Urinary retention
• Blood at the urethral meatus
• Perineal hematoma (Butterfly hematoma)

Note: Urinary bladder rupture occurs due to an injury to the suprapubic region. Extraperitoneal bladder rupture is more common and associated with pelvic fracture. Intraperitoneal bladder rupture is caused by a blow or a fall on the distended bladder. It manifests as sudden severe pain in the hypogastrium and syncope.
questions.learning: Bulbar urethra — The given clinical scenario with a history of an astride injury, blood at the tip of the meatus, and inability to pass urine are all suggestive of an injury to the bulbar urethra.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 51-year-old lady presents with complaints of a mass in the right breast. On examination, the mass was larger than 2cm and ipsilateral mobile axillary lymph nodes were present. What is the staging, considering the mass is malignant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. cT4N1M0

The clinical scenario of a 51-year-old lady with a breast mass >2cm, lymph node involvement (N1), and the image showing an ulcerative mass near the nipple of the right breast (T4), is clinically suggestive of inflammatory breast carcinoma. Its likely staging is cT4N1M0

Inflammatory breast carcinoma (stage T4) is an aggressive form of locally advanced breast cancer (LABC) and is associated with the worst prognosis among all subtypes of breast cancer. It accounts for <3% of breast cancers. It is characterized by skin changes of brawny induration, erythema, and edema (peau d’orange). The term peau d’orange describes the orange-peel appearance of the skin resulting from edema and dimpling at sites of hair follicles.

In order to determine the best course of treatment for a patient with IBC, it is important to stage cancer. Staging is the process of determining the extent to which cancer has spread within the breast and to other parts of the body. Some prefixes and suffixes are used with the cTNM (clinical) and pTNM (pathologic) staging systems to designate special cases. These do not affect the stage group but indicate that they must be analyzed separately. The “y” prefix, denotes patients who have received systemic therapy before surgery. In this patient, since the staging is being done clinically, "c" is added as a prefix.

The diagnostic criteria for inflammatory breast cancer are -

*

Rapid onset of breast erythema, edema and/or peau d’orange, and/or warm breast (with or without an underlying palpable mass)

*

Duration of history no more than six months

*

Erythema occupies at least one-third of the breast

*

Pathologic confirmation of invasive carcinoma

The pathologic hallmark is the presence of tumor cells within dermal lymphatics in skin biopsy specimens, but it is not a prerequisite for diagnosis. Mammography may be normal or show skin thickening. A PET-CT scan should be considered at the time of diagnosis to rule out concurrent metastatic disease.

Axillary nodal metastases are common, and there is a significant risk for distant metastases.

Combined-modality treatment is used, which includes

* Neoadjuvant chemotherapy

* Modified radical mastectomy

* Radiation therapy

* Hormonal therapy (for ER-positive tumors)

* Trastuzumab (for HER-2-positive tumors)

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Based on the combination of colicky abdominal pain, palpable purpura over the buttocks and extensor surfaces, and renal involvement (proteinuria with microscopic hematuria) in a 7-year-old child, the most likely diagnosis is Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis).
questions.explanation: The combination of a characteristic palpable purpuric rash (on buttocks and lower limbs), cramping abdominal pain, and signs of renal involvement (hematuria and proteinuria) in a young child is the hallmark presentation of Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP). HSP is an IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis that often follows a viral upper respiratory infection. Systemic lupus erythematosus (Option A) is much less common in a 7-year-old and typically presents with a malar rash and multi-organ involvement. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (Option C) presents with acute nephritic syndrome (hematuria/hypertension) following a throat infection but lacks the systemic purpuric rash and abdominal pain. Hemolytic uremic syndrome (Option D) is characterized by a triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure, usually following bloody diarrhea. Given the classic rash distribution and clinical tetrad, HSP is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The combination of a characteristic palpable purpuric rash (on buttocks and lower limbs), cramping abdominal pain, and signs of renal involvement (hematuria and proteinuria) in a young child is the hallmark presentation of Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 19-year-old male with a history of chronic smoking presents with fever and a painful swelling below the left ear near the cheek region. He also has difficulty speaking or swallowing and complains of mild testicular pain. Based on this clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation of fever and a painful lump beneath the ear (parotitis) is characteristic of Mumps, an acute viral infection caused by a rubulavirus. The crucial clinical clue is the "mild testicular pain," which suggests orchitis, a common complication of mumps in post-pubertal males. Cervical tuberculosis (Option A) usually presents with chronic, painless "cold" lymphadenopathy. Diphtheria (Option B) is associated with a greyish-white pharyngeal membrane and severe "bull neck" swelling. Lymphoma (Option D) typically presents with painless, rubbery, and generalized lymphadenopathy rather than acute painful parotid swelling. Smoking is a distractor here, as it does not directly cause this acute constellation of symptoms. Mumps is generally a self-limiting disease, but management involves supportive care and monitoring for complications like meningitis or pancreatitis
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation of fever and a painful lump beneath the ear (parotitis) is characteristic of Mumps, an acute viral infection caused by a rubulavirus.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Who conducts inquest in Police custodial death?
questions.explanation: An inquest is a preliminary investigation to determine the cause and circumstances of an unnatural death. Under the laws of India (specifically Section 176 of the CrPC), a Judicial Magistrate is legally required to conduct an inquest in any case of death that occurs while a person is in police custody. This is a critical safeguard designed to ensure transparency, impartiality, and to prevent potential human rights abuses or cover-ups by the police force themselves. A higher police official (Option A) may conduct an internal departmental inquiry, but the official legal inquest must be independent. Medical examiners (Option C) and Coroners (Option D) are systems used in other countries like the US or UK, but in India, the role is filled by Magistrates or the Police. This mandatory judicial oversight is fundamental to the rule of law and the protection of the constitutional rights of individuals, even those who have been lawfully detained
questions.learning: An inquest is a preliminary investigation to determine the cause and circumstances of an unnatural death. Under the laws of India (specifically Section 176 of the CrPC), a Judicial Magistrate is legally required to conduct an inquest in any case of death…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following is not a wound prone to the development of tetanus?
options: Wound on forearm contaminated with soil
Donor site of a split-thickness skin graft
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Donor site of a split-thickness skin graft

Clostridium tetani spores are found in soil and can enter wounds, particularly those with devitalized tissue, contamination, or poor oxygenation.

• (a) Compound fracture of tibia — Tetanus-prone: Open fractures involve tissue damage and contamination, providing favorable conditions for C. tetani.
• (b) Forearm wound contaminated with soil — Tetanus-prone: Soil contamination increases the risk of inoculation with C. tetani spores.
• (c) Donor site of split-thickness skin graft — Not typically tetanus-prone → Correct: It is a clean, surgically created superficial wound without the typical anaerobic environment or soil contamination associated with tetanus.
• (d) Dog bite over abdominal wall — Tetanus-prone: Animal bites are contaminated wounds and are considered potential tetanus-prone wounds.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: All of the following are risk factors of vulval cancer except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vulval hamartoma

Vulval hamartoma is not a risk factor for vulval cancer.

Vulval cancer is a rare genital tract cancer that may be divided into preinvasive lesions and invasive carcinoma. 90% of the invasive carcinomas are squamous cell carcinoma and are usually present on the labia majora. The risk factors for both types are:

• Chronic vulval irritation
• Immunosuppressive conditions such as pregnancy, HIV infection
• Smoking
• Condyloma (anogenital warts)
• Sexually transmitted diseases
• Dystrophies
questions.learning: Vulval hamartoma Vulval hamartoma is not a risk factor for vulval cancer. Vulval cancer is a rare genital tract cancer that may be divided into preinvasive lesions and invasive carcinoma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the sinus that is labeled in the provided image.
questions.explanation: The paranasal sinuses are air-filled cavities within the skull bones surrounding the nasal cavity. The arrow in the provided image points to the largest paranasal sinus, located within the body of the maxilla, inferior to the orbits. This is the maxillary sinus (Antrum of Highmore). The frontal sinuses (Option A) are located superior to the orbits within the frontal bone. The ethmoid sinuses (Option C) are a complex of small air cells located between the orbits and the upper nasal cavity. The pyriform sinus (Option B) is not a paranasal sinus; it is a recess in the laryngopharynx, making it an anatomical distractor. The maxillary sinus is clinically significant as it is frequently involved in sinusitis, and its close proximity to the roots of the upper molar teeth means that dental infections can sometimes spread to the sinus. Identifying these structures on imaging or diagrams is fundamental for diagnosing common otorhinolaryngological conditions and planning surgical drainage procedures
questions.learning: The paranasal sinuses are air-filled cavities within the skull bones surrounding the nasal cavity. The arrow in the provided image points to the largest paranasal sinus, located within the body of the maxilla, inferior to the orbits.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The major contributor to demographic burden is __________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased old age dependency ratio

Demographic burden refers to an increase in the total dependency ratio, mostly caused by an increased old-age dependency ratio.

The term demographic bonus denotes the decline in dependency ratio due to declining fertility.

Note :

A decline in the dependency ratio especially the young age dependency ratio has been identified to be a key factor underlying the rapid economic development.

Pearl PF0983: Demographic Process and Cycle

* Demographic process

* Fertility

* Mortality

* Marriage

* Migration

* Social Mobility

* Demographic cycle

* Stage 1 : High stationary

* High birth rate and high death rate render the population stationary.

* Narrow demographic gap.

* Stage 2 : Early expanding

* Death rate declines and birth rate remains unchanged

* Demographic gap starts increasing and then becomes maximum

* Stage 3 : Late expanding

* Death rate decline further and birth rate falls

* India is in this stage, currently

* Demographic gap starts declining

* Stage 4 : Low stationary

* Low birth rate and low death rate renders the population stationary

* Narrow demographic gap

* Stage 5 : Declining

* Population begins to decline as birth rate is lower than death rate

* Demographic gap is negative
questions.learning: Increased old age dependency ratio Demographic burden refers to an increase in the total dependency ratio, mostly caused by an increased old-age dependency ratio.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A female patient presents with difficulty ingesting liquids more than solids. What is the most likely characteristic finding on imaging?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rat tail appearance

The clinical scenario of a female patient having more difficulty swallowing liquids than solids suggests achalasia cardia, with the characteristic imaging finding being the Rat tail sign.

Achalasia is a primary oesophagal motility disorder. It is characterized by the absence of oesophagal peristalsis and impaired lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation in response to swallowing. These abnormalities cause a functional obstruction at the gastroesophageal junction.

Esophageal manometry shows:

* Incomplete LES relaxation in response to swallowing.

* High resting LES pressure.

* Absent esophageal peristalsis.

On performing a timed barium study, barium will be retained for more than five minutes. The fluoroscopic examination will reveal a dilated oesophagus that tapers to form a bird's beak at the gastroesophageal junction as seen in the image above. Endoscopy and biopsy are usually carried out to rule out cancer. 24-hour pH monitoring is used in the diagnosis of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

Medical management with sublingual nitroglycerin, nitrates, and calcium-channel blockers for symptomatic relief. Pneumatic dilatation and Botox injection

Surgical management is the treatment of choice :

* Laparoscopic Heller's myotomy is the definitive management - The major complication associated with this procedure is gastro-oesophageal reflux. So it is best to combine it with partial anterior fundoplication (Heller–Dor operation).

* Peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) is a recently introduced, advanced natural-orifice approach for myotomy.

* Open Esophageal Myotomy - rarely done.

Other options:

Option A: Apple core sign is characteristically seen in the barium enema of carcinoma colon as shown below.

Option B: Barium enema radiograph of diverticulosis shows multiple barium-coated outpouchings from the colonic wall and gives the appearance of a saw-tooth as shown below.

Option C: Crohn's disease is an inflammatory bowel disease that shows the string sign of Kantor on barium enema as shown below.

Pearl PF0313: Achalasia Cardia

Achalasia is a rare disease caused by the loss of ganglion cells within the esophageal myenteric plexus.

Their absence leads to increased tone of the lower esophageal sphincter, impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES), and absent peristalsis.

Achalasia is the only true motility disorder of the esophagus.

Primary achalasia is due to ganglion cell degeneration and is thought to be due to an autoimmune process attributable to latent infection with human herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV1) combined with genetic susceptibility.

Secondary achalasia may arise in Chaga's disease

Clinical features:

* dysphagia (solid and liquid food)

* regurgitation

* chest pain

* weight loss

* bronchitis, pneumonia, or lung abscess from aspiration

Differential diagnosis: Diffuse esophageal spasm, Chagas’ disease, and pseudoachalasia

On barium swallow: Bird beak-appearance

Investigation of choice: Manometry (most sensitive)

Treatment: Pneumatic dilatation and Heller myotomy

Pearl PF0315: Manometric findings in oesophageal disorders

Manometric Findings in Nutcracker Esophagus

* Peristaltic esophageal contractions 2 standard deviations above normal

* Amplitude > 180 mmHg and duration > 7seconds.

* Normal peristaltic sequence

Manometric Findings in Diffuse Esophageal Spasm

* Simultaneous, multipeaked contractions of high amplitude (>120 mm Hg) or long duration (>2.5 sec)

* These erratic contractions occur after more than 20% of wet swallows.

* Intermittent normal peristalsis

Manometric Findings in Hypertensive Lower Esophageal Sphincter-

* Elevated LES pressure > 26mmHg and normal relaxation of LES

* The esophageal body may be hyper-peristaltic or normal.

Manometric findings in Achalasia Cardia

* Incomplete LES relaxation

* Aperistalsis in the esophageal body

* Elevated LES pressure ≥26 mmHg

* Increased intraesophageal baseline pressures relative to gastric baseline

Manometric findings in ineffective esophageal motility disorders

* Decreased or absent amplitude of esophageal peristalsis (<30 mmHg)

* Increased number of non-transmitted contractions
questions.learning: Rat tail appearance — The clinical scenario of a female patient having more difficulty swallowing liquids than solids suggests achalasia cardia, with the characteristic imaging finding being the Rat tail sign.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under the Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK), how frequently are health check-ups conducted for children in the 9–18 years age group?
questions.explanation: The Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) is an Indian initiative aimed at the early identification and management of the "4 Ds": Defects at birth, Diseases, Deficiencies, and Developmental delays including disability. For older children and adolescents aged 9 to 18 years who are enrolled in schools, health screenings are scheduled once a year. These check-ups are typically conducted by mobile health teams consisting of medical officers and paramedics who visit the schools. Options B, C, and D are incorrect frequencies for this specific age group under the national guidelines. For younger children (0 to 6 years), the screening frequency is higher, occurring bi-annually at Anganwadi centers. Annual screening for school children is designed to detect conditions like vision impairment, hearing loss, or learning disabilities that might interfere with their education and long-term development. Early detection allows for timely referral to District Early Intervention Centers (DEICs) for comprehensive management and rehabilitation
questions.learning: The Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) is an Indian initiative aimed at the early identification and management of the "4 Ds": Defects at birth, Diseases, Deficiencies, and Developmental delays including disability.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 3-year-old boy presents with mental retardation and an inability to walk. The funduscopy image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tay-Sachs disease

The given clinical scenario, along with the fundoscopy image showing a macular cherry-red spot, indicates the most likely diagnosis to be Tay-Sachs disease.

Tay-Sachs disease is a lysosomal storage disease caused by the deficiency of β-hexosaminidase. It can present during infancy with macrocephaly, increased startle reaction, gradual loss of motor skills, and a macular cherry-red spot. Affected children usually die by the age of 10–15 years.

It is of two types—juvenile-onset and adult-onset. The symptoms of the juvenile-onset form include ataxia and dementia. Dysarthria, lower motor neuron signs, and psychiatric disorders are common in the adult-onset type.

Other options:

Options B - Hunter disease (mucopolysaccharidosis II) is an X-linked disorder that arises due to the deficiency of iduronate 2-sulfatase. Short stature, joint stiffness, and intellectual disability are the features.

Option C - Hurler syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis I) is an autosomal recessive condition that affects multiple organs. Presentation is usually at 6–24 months with corneal clouding, coarse facial features, joint stiffness, and skeletal dysplasia. Glaucoma, retinal degeneration, and nasal discharge are the other features. The condition is generally fatal.

Option D - Gaucher disease is a glycolipid storage disorder that can present with hepatosplenomegaly, mental retardation, and erosion of long bones. It is caused by the deficiency of β-glucosidase. The Gaucher cell has a wrinkled-paper appearance due to intracytoplasmic inclusions, which is a characteristic feature.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Orthotolidine test is used to determine ________
options: Free and combined chlorine in water
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Free and combined chlorine in water

Orthotolidine (OT) test is used to determine free and combined chlorine in water.

Pearl PF0273: Chlorination of Water

* Chlorination is widely used for large scale purification of water and for drinking water.

* It is bactericidal and moderately virucidal but not sporicidal, except in high doses.

* Alongside its anti-pathogenic attributes, it oxidizes iron, manganese and hydrogen sulphide. It also destroys some taste and odor producing components. It controls algae and slime organisms and aids in coagulation.

* Action of chlorine:

* Hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid are formed when chlorine is added to water. Hypochlorous acid ionizes to form hydrogen and hypochlorite ions.

* H2O + Cl2 → HCl + HOCl
HOCl → H + OCl

* The disinfecting action of chlorine is predominantly due to hypochlorous acid. Hypochlorous acid is the most effective form of chlorine and it is almost 70 – 80 times more effective than hypochlorite ions.

* Chlorine acts best in water that has a pH of around 7.

* Principles of chlorination:

* The water to be disinfected must be clear of turbidity as turbidity impedes efficient chlorination.

* The chlorine demand of water is the difference between the amount of chlorine added to the water and the amount of residual chlorine remaining at the end of a specific period of contact (usually 60 minutes) at a given temperature and pH of the water. This has to be estimated before chlorination is done.

* The point at which the chlorine demand of water is met is called the breakpoint. It is beyond this that residual free chlorine begins to appear.

* Contact period of free chlorine for at least one hour is required to kill bacteria and viruses.

* Minimum recommended concentration of free chlorine is 0.5 mg/litre for one hour. Free residual chlorine provides a margin of safety against microbial contamination that occurs in storage or transport.

* The sum of the chlorine demand of the specific water plus free residual chlorine of 0.5 mg/litre constitutes the correct dose of chlorine to be applied.

* Methods of chlorination

* Chlorine gas: It is the first choice as it is cheap, quick and efficient in action and easy to apply. Special chlorinating equipments like Paterson’s chloronome are used for application of chlorine gas.

* Chloramines: These loose compounds of chlorine and ammonia give more persistent forms of residual chlorine. They have slow action and thus are not widely used.

* Perchloron or high test hypochlorite (H.T.H.): It is a calcium compound that has 60 – 70% of available chlorine.

* Break point chlorination:

* The point at which the chlorine demand of water is met is called the breakpoint.

* Free chlorine (HOCl and OCl) appears when chlorine is added beyond the breakpoint.

* In other words, at the breakpoint, if chlorine is added, then all the combined chlorines have been completely destroyed and free residual chlorines begin to appear.

* This corresponding dosage to achieve appearance of free residual chlorine is called breakpoint dosage and this method is called breakpoint chlorination.

* It is also called controlled superchlorination

* Superchlorination followed by dechlorination is used to disinfect highly polluted waters whose quality fluctuates greatly.

* Orthotolidine (OT) test:

* It is a test for chlorination and determines free and combined chlorine in water, rapidly and accurately.

* The reagent used is analytical grade Orthotolidine dissolved in 10% solution of hydrochloric acid.

* When added to water which contains chlorine, it turns yellow with varying intensity. This is faster in the presence of free chlorine and slower in the presence of combined chlorines.

* Orthotolidine - arsenite (OTA) test:

* This is a modification of the OT test which nullifies the errors caused due to interfering substances like iron, nitrites, manganese, etc.

* It determines free and combined chlorines separately.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: FISH technique helps to identify all except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Point mutation

Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) is not useful in identifying point mutation. Point mutations are identified by other means like sequencing studies and restriction fragment length polymorphism.

FISH is a method of molecular analysis of genetic lesions involving large deletions, duplications, or more complex rearrangements that are not readily amenable to detection using polymerase chain reaction or DNA sequencing approaches.

FISH uses DNA probes that recognize sequences specific to particular chromosomal regions. To perform FISH, large fragments of cloned genomic DNA spanning up to 200 kb are labeled with fluorescent dyes and applied to metaphase chromosome preparations or interphase nuclei. The probe hybridizes to its homologous genomic sequence and thus labels a specific chromosomal region that can be visualized under a fluorescent microscope.

FISH can be performed on prenatal samples, peripheral blood cells, touch preparations from cancer biopsies, and even fixed archival tissue sections. It is used to detect numeric abnormalities of chromosomes (aneuploidy), subtle microdeletions and complex translocations that are not demonstrable by routine karyotyping, and gene amplification (e.g., HER2 in breast cancer or NMYC amplification in neuroblastomas).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the given histology slide:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pancreas

The above image shows pancreatic islet cells. Islet of Langerhans makes up the endocrine part of the pancreas.

Islets are characterized by secretory cells supported by reticulin fibers, and containing numerous fenestrated capillaries. There is a delicate capsule around each islet. They are paler than the surrounding exocrine cells, as they have less rough endoplasmic reticulum. The image given below shows the histology of the pancreas:

The islets of Langerhans contain four major and two minor cell types:

Four main types are β, α, δ, and PP (pancreatic polypeptide) cells:

* α or A cells- located peripherally and secrete glucagon

* β or B cells- located centrally and produce insulin

* δ or D cells- scattered between beta cells and secrete somatostatin

* PP cells- are present in islets and also in the exocrine pancreas. They secrete a pancreatic polypeptide, which exerts several gastrointestinal effects, such as stimulation of secretion of gastric and intestinal enzymes and inhibition of intestinal motility.

Minor cell types:

* D1 cells secrete vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), a hormone that induces glycogenolysis and hyperglycemia. It also stimulates gastrointestinal fluid secretion and causes secretory diarrhea.

* Enterochromaffin cells synthesize serotonin and are the source of pancreatic tumors that cause carcinoid syndrome.

Other options:

Option A: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs. The structure of lymph nodes consists of an outer cortex and inner medulla. The cortex contains an aggregation of B-lymphocytes (primary follicles) and quiescent secondary follicles with a pale central germinal center.

The inner medulla consists of medullary cords (lymphocytes and plasma cells) and medullary sinuses. Between the cortex and medulla, there is an ill-defined zone called the paracortex, which contains T lymphocytes. The image given below shows the histology of the lymph node:

Option B: Glomerulus is a rounded tuft of anastomosing capillaries. The glomerular capillary wall is the filtering membrane and consists of fenestrated endothelial cells, basement membrane, and visceral epithelial cells called podocytes, which contain foot processes. The image given below shows the histology of the glomerulus:

Option C: Spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ. It contains round white pulp surrounded by red pulp. The white pulp is made up of aggregations of lymphocytes that surround a small artery or arterioles.

The red pulp is a modified lymphoid tissue infiltrated with all the cells of circulating blood. It is like a sponge permeated by spaces (splenic sinusoids) lined by reticular cells. The zone of red pulp immediately surrounding white pulp is the marginal zone. This zone has a rich network of sinusoids. The image given below shows the histology of the spleen:

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia encloses all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sternocleidomastoid

All the above structures are enclosed by the pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia except sternocleidomastoid. It is enclosed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia.

The deep cervical fascia of the neck is organized into the following layers:

• The investing layer, which surrounds all structures in the neck
• The prevertebral layer, which surrounds the vertebral column and the deep muscles associated with the back.
• The pretracheal layer, which encloses the viscera of the neck
• The carotid sheath, which receives a contribution from the other three fascial layers

In the neck, the pretracheal fascia covers the strap muscles i.e sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid. It splits to enclose the thyroid gland. It also surrounds the trachea and the esophagus including the recurrent laryngeal nerve present in the groove between them.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding the murmur of Patent Ductus Arteriosus: 1. It is a continuous ‘machinery’ murmur. 2. There is a late diastolic accentuation. 3. It is maximal in the second left intercostal space below the clavicle. 4. With the development of Eisenmenger Syndrome, the murmur becomes louder and rumbling in character. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 3

• 1. Continuous “machinery” murmur: Correct

• PDA produces a continuous murmur because blood flows from the aorta to the pulmonary artery during both systole and diastole.
• It is classically described as a machinery murmur.

• 2. Late diastolic accentuation: Incorrect

• The murmur is generally continuous with systolic accentuation, rather than specifically late-diastolic accentuation.

• 3. Maximal at the second left intercostal space below the clavicle: Correct

• The murmur is best heard at the left upper sternal border / second left intercostal space, beneath the left clavicle.

• 4. Becomes louder and rumbling with Eisenmenger syndrome: Incorrect

• As pulmonary vascular resistance rises and the shunt decreases or reverses, the PDA murmur becomes softer and may eventually disappear.
• A prominent continuous murmur requires a significant left-to-right pressure gradient.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient on anti-cancer therapy developed an infection. Blood analysis revealed neutropenia. Which of the following drug is likely to be effective in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Filgrastim

Filgrastim is the drug used in the treatment of chemotherapy-induced neutropenia.

Filgrastim is a recombinant human G-CSF(granulocyte-colony stimulating factor), that stimulates CFU-G(colony-forming unit- granulocyte) to increase neutrophil production. It is administered subcutaneously or by slow intravenous infusion. It is indicated in:

* The treatment of severe neutropenia after autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation and high-dose cancer chemotherapy.

* The treatment of severe congenital neutropenias.

* The treatment of neutropenia of patients with AIDS receiving zidovudine.

Important adverse reactions include bone pain, local skin reaction, and cutaneous necrotizing vasculitis.

Other options:

Option A: Romiplostim is a thrombopoietin receptor agonist. It is used in the management of immune thrombocytopenic purpura(ITP).

Option B: Oprelvekin is a recombinant human IL-11. It stimulates hematopoiesis. It is used in the treatment of thrombocytopenia due to non-myeloid malignancies. Important adverse effects are fluid retention, tachycardia, palpitation, edema, and shortness of breath.

Option D: Epoetin alfa is a recombinant human erythropoietin analogue that stimulates red blood cell production. It is used in the treatment of anaemias associated with surgery, chronic kidney disease, AIDS, cancer chemotherapy, prematurity, and certain chronic inflammatory conditions.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: While performing the USG assessment of a woman at 28 weeks of gestation, you note her amniotic fluid index to be 12.8. When does this parameter reach its maximum value in a normal pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 34 weeks of gestation

The amniotic fluid index (AFI) is a measure of the amniotic volume which is maximum at 34 weeks of gestation.

The volume of amniotic fluid each week is variable. The volume gradually increases till 32-34 weeks of gestation. At 34 weeks, it is maximum and thereafter it starts declining till term.

Amniotic fluid volume is a passive reflector of the fetal condition. Its volume is determined by the following:

Pathway
Volume in ml

Fetal urination
+1000

Fetal swallowing
-750

Fetal lung fluid secretion
+350

Intramembranous flow across fetal vessels on the placental surface
-400

Early in pregnancy, amnionic fluid arises mainly from a transudate of plasma either from the fetal skin or across the uterine decidua and placenta. Fetal urine production becomes a major component in the second trimester.

Any alteration in fetal homeostasis, caused by fetal and maternal conditions, affects the amniotic fluid volume. Thus, AFI is measured as a part of the biophysical score.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A blood sample from a patient with diabetes is collected and stored in the container shown. Which substance is added to the blood sample in this container?
questions.explanation: The container shown is a grey-top vacutainer, which is specifically used for blood glucose and lactate estimation. The additive in this tube is Sodium fluoride (NaF), which serves as a potent antiglycolytic agent. It inhibits the enzyme enolase in the glycolytic pathway, preventing red blood cells from consuming the glucose in the sample post-collection. This ensures that the measured glucose level accurately reflects the patient's state at the time of the draw. EDTA (Option B) is in purple-top tubes for hematology. Sodium citrate (Option C) is in light blue-top tubes for coagulation studies. Heparin (Option D) is in green-top tubes for clinical chemistry and arterial blood gases. Without NaF, blood glucose levels drop by approximately 5-10% per hour at room temperature due to cellular metabolism. This additive is essential for the accurate diagnosis and monitoring of diabetes mellitus in clinical practice

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During a lactation consultation, a mother reports experiencing cramp-like breast pain while breastfeeding. Which hormone is primarily responsible for causing these cramps?
questions.explanation: The sensation of "breast cramps" or tingling felt by a mother during breastfeeding is part of the milk ejection reflex. When the infant suckles at the nipple, sensory nerves send signals to the hypothalamus, triggering the release of oxytocin from the posterior pituitary. Oxytocin then travels to the breast, where it causes the contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the alveoli to squeeze milk into the ducts. These rhythmic contractions are often perceived by the mother as cramping. Prolactin (Option C) is responsible for milk production (galactopoiesis), not the mechanical ejection or cramping. Estrogen (Option B) and Progesterone (Option A) are involved in breast growth during pregnancy but actually inhibit milk production until their levels drop after delivery. Therefore, oxytocin is the definitive hormone responsible for the mechanical contractions and associated "let-down" cramps during lactation

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Killian's dehiscence is located between which two structures?
questions.explanation: Killian's dehiscence is a triangular area of relative muscular weakness located in the posterior wall of the lower pharynx. It is specifically situated between the oblique fibers of the thyropharyngeus muscle and the transverse fibers of the cricopharyngeus muscle, both of which are parts of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor. This area is clinically significant because it is the most common site for the formation of a Zenker's diverticulum. Increased pressure during swallowing can cause the mucosa to herniate through this weak point. Options A, B, and D are incorrect as they involve the palatopharyngeus or salpingopharyngeus, which are internal muscles of the pharynx and do not form this specific anatomical landmark. Patients with a Zenker's diverticulum often present with dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, and halitosis. Surgical or endoscopic management often requires the division of the cricopharyngeus muscle (cricopharyngeal myotomy) to relieve the pressure at Killian's dehiscence

questions.text: Which of the following is a cause of sensorineural hearing loss?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Labyrinthitis

In the above options, labyrinthitis is a cause of sensorineural hearing loss while all others are causes of conductive hearing loss.

Causes of sensorineural hearing loss:

* Congenital

* Anomalies of the inner ear or the hearing apparatus due to prenatal or perinatal factors

* Acquired

* Labyrinthitis—viral, bacterial, or spirochaetal

* Trauma to labyrinth or VIIIth nerve

* Noise-induced hearing loss

* Ototoxic drugs

* Presbycusis

* Ménière’s disease

* Acoustic neuroma

* Systemic disorders-diabetes, autoimmune disorders, multiple sclerosis

Causes of conductive hearing loss:

* Congenital

* Meatal atresia

* Fixation of stapes footplate/malleus head

* Ossicular discontinuity

* Congenital cholesteatoma

* Acquired

* External ear

* Obstruction in the ear canal-wax, foreign body, furuncle

* Middle ear

* Perforation of tympanic membrane

* Fluid in the middle ear-acute otitis media, serous otitis media

* Tumors in the middle ear

* Disruption of ossicles-chronic suppurative otitis media, cholesteatoma

* Fixation of ossicles-otosclerosis, tympanosclerosis, adhesive otitis media

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient was admitted to the ICU 48 hours after the fracture of the femur. The saturation of oxygen in the rebreathing unit was 100% but his SpO2 remained at 60%. The patient is in a state of confusion. Chest radiograph showed lung fields to be clear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fat embolism

The most likely diagnosis of the above clinical scenario is a fat embolism. The presence of respiratory insufficiency and altered mental status following a long bone fracture (fracture of the femur) favors the diagnosis.

Fat embolism syndrome results from the presence of numerous fat emboli within the microcirculation. It most commonly occurs after the fracture of the long bone or pelvis. They present with non-specific symptoms like tachypnea, tachycardia, and fever that manifest within 24- 48 hours after the injury. Damage to the microvasculature of various organs leads to :

* Mild hypoxia to rapidly progressing respiratory failure.

* Depression of the central nervous system.

* Petechial rashes

* Hemorrhagic lesions of the retina.

Pearl PF1166: Gurd's criteria for diagnosing fat embolism syndrome

Major criteria

* Axillary or subconjunctival petechiae

* Hypoxemia with PaO2 <60 mmHg, FIO2 < 0.4

* CNS depression disproportionate to the hypoxemia

* Pulmonary edema

Minor criteria

* Tachycardia (HR >110 beats per minute)

* Pyrexia (temp >38.50C)

* Emboli visible in retina

* Fat globules in urine

* Fat globules in sputum

* Unexplanied drop in hematocrit or platelet count

* Increased ESR

At least one major criterion and four minor criteria are required to make a diagnosis of fat embolism syndrome.
questions.learning: Fat embolism — The most likely diagnosis of the above clinical scenario is a fat embolism. The presence of respiratory insufficiency and altered mental status following a long bone fracture (fracture of the femur) favors the diagnosis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following vitamins is breast milk deficient in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin K

Breast milk is deficient in vitamin K.

Therefore infants have to be supplemented with vitamin K to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

The composition of breast milk varies at different time points of lactation to suit the needs of the baby.

* Colostrum is secreted in small quantities during the first 3 to 4 days. It is thick, and yellow and contains many antibodies, immune-competent cells, and vitamins A, D, E, and K.

* Transitional milk is the one that is seen after 3-4 days until 2 weeks and has an increased fat and sugar content while the protein and immunoglobulin content reduces.

* Mature milk is secreted after transitional milk. It is essential for the baby's optimum growth as it contains all the nutrients. It is thinner and more watery.

Foremilk is the one that is secreted during the initial feed. It is watery and quenches the thirst of the baby. It is rich in proteins, sugar, vitamins, minerals, and water. Hindmilk is rich in fat and provides energy. It gives a sense of satiety to the baby. Hindmilk comes towards the end of the feed.

Components of breast milk and diseases they protect against:

Components of breast milk
Protection against

Lysozyme

• Escherichia coli, Salmonella
• Entamoeba histolytica

Lactoferrin

• E. coli, Shigella, Salmonella
• E. histolytica, Giardia lamblia
• Plasmodium falciparum
• Rotavirus

Bifidus factor
E. coli, Shigella, Salmonella

Low levels of para-aminobenzoic acid
Plasmodium

Breastmilk is also deficient in vitamin D and exclusively breastfed infants can develop vitamin D deficiency unless adequately supplemented.

Human milk is a rich source of vitamin C and contains around 5-15mg/100cal. Vitamin C is found in higher levels in breast milk than in cow milk.
questions.learning: Vitamin K Breast milk is deficient in vitamin K. Therefore infants have to be supplemented with vitamin K to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 52-year-old male patient comes with complaints of abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. A peripheral blood smear reveals macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils and an endoscopy reveals atrophic gastritis. Which of the following conditions is likely to be seen this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B12 deficiency

The given findings are suggestive of pernicious anemia, which is associated with atrophic gastritis and vitamin B12 deficiency.

Anemic patient with a peripheral smear showing macrocytic RBCs and hypersegmented neutrophils are important characteristic features of megaloblastic anemia. Vitamin B12 and folic acid deficiency are the main causes of megaloblastic anemia.

Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune disease characterized by the presence of autoantibodies which impairs the production or activity of the intrinsic factor (IF). This is required for the uptake of vitamin B12. There are three types of autoantibodies namely, type I, II, and III. The action of each of these include:

• Autoantibody type I prevents the binding of vitamin B12 to the intinsic factor (IF).
• Autoantibody type II prevents the binding of vitamin B12-IF complex to the ileal receptors.
• Autoantibody type III acts against the α and β subunits of the gastric proton pump, which impairs the production of intrinsic factor.

These patients also develop chronic atrophic gastritis, characterized by loss of parietal cells, infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells and megaloblastic changes in mucosal cells.
questions.learning: Vitamin B12 deficiency — The given findings are suggestive of pernicious anemia, which is associated with atrophic gastritis and vitamin B12 deficiency.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are risk factors for the development of pancreatic cancer? 1. Cigarette smoking 2. Diabetes mellitus 3. Caucasian ethnicity 4. Male gender Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive malignancy with a poor prognosis because it is often diagnosed at an advanced stage. Several modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors increase the likelihood of developing pancreatic cancer, with cigarette smoking being the most important modifiable risk factor.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Cigarette smoking ✅

• Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor, increasing the risk of pancreatic cancer by 2–3 times.

• 2. Diabetes mellitus ✅

• Long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus is an established risk factor. Conversely, new-onset diabetes in older adults may be an early manifestation of pancreatic cancer.

• 3. Caucasian ethnicity ❌

• Pancreatic cancer is more common in African Americans than in Caucasians; therefore, Caucasian ethnicity is not considered a risk factor.

• 4. Male gender ✅

• The incidence is slightly higher in males, partly due to greater exposure to smoking and occupational carcinogens.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive malignancy with a poor prognosis because it is often diagnosed at an advanced stage.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which ligament is tested in the following test?
questions.explanation: The image illustrates the Anterior Drawer Test, a common clinical maneuver used to evaluate the integrity of the Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL). To perform the test, the knee is flexed to 90 degrees, and the examiner pulls the tibia forward while stabilizing the femur. Excessive forward displacement of the tibia indicates an ACL tear. The Posterior Cruciate Ligament (PCL) (Option B) is assessed using the Posterior Drawer Test, where the tibia is pushed backward instead. The Medial Collateral Ligament (MCL) (Option C) is tested using the valgus stress test to check for gapping on the inner side of the knee. The Lateral Collateral Ligament (LCL) (Option D) is evaluated with the varus stress test to check the outer side of the joint. Because the image shows the tibia being pulled anteriorly, the ACL is the correct target of this specific test

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 58-year-old woman was undergoing cholecystectomy. During the procedure, the resident accidentally advanced the scissors along the superior border of the epiploic foramen causing injury. Which of the following structures is likely to be injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Caudate lobe of liver

The superior border of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) is formed by the caudate lobe of the liver. It is likely to be injured in this case.

Epiploic foramen is a vertical slit of about 3 cm behind the free right border of the lesser omentum. It connects the lesser sac to the greater sac.

Clinical note: Pringle maneuver (as shown below) is a technique where the free margin of the lesser omentum is compressed to obtain rapid control of bleeding from the hepatic artery and portal vein in liver trauma and surgery.
questions.learning: Caudate lobe of liver — The superior border of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) is formed by the caudate lobe of the liver. It is likely to be injured in this case.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Revised A patient comes with a history of category 3 dog bites. He received prophylaxis for a monkey bite 6 months back. What is the next step in management? RIG- Rabies immunoglobulin
options: Wound cleaning+ rabies vaccine on day 0 & 3
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Wound cleaning+ rabies vaccine on day 0 & 3

This patient should receive 2 doses of vaccine on days 0 & 3 as he has received a prior course of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) > 3 months ago.

In India, monkeys are known to transmit rabies. Hence the national rabies control program advises a full course of PEP for monkey bites. This patient who was bitten by a monkey 6 months back would have received PEP for rabies.

Management of a new dog bite in a previously immunized individual with either pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) or post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is as follows:

* Category I: Wound treatment only

* Category II/ III:

* Wound treatment with soap and running water for 15 min and apply antiseptic

* Receive Anti-rabies vaccine (ARV) 2 doses ID (0.1 ml, 1 site)/ 2 doses IM (1 VIAL, 1 site) on days 0 and 3.

Rabies immunoglobulin is not given for any category in case they have completed a full course of PEP.

*Note: In developing countries like India, the vaccination status of animals alone, doesn't play a significant role in determining the initiation of prophylaxis in humans.

Pearl PF1934: Rabies vaccines and immunoglobulins schedules

According to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India:

WHO category II or III exposures should receive post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) immediately.

One intradermal (ID) dose is 0.1 mL of vaccine and one intramuscular (IM) dose is an entire vial of vaccine, irrespective of the vial size.

Should a vaccine dose be delayed for any reason, the PEP schedule should be resumed (not restarted).

Rabies Immunoglobulin(RIG):

* Passive immunization

* Single-dose; after initiation of PEP and not beyond 7 days after the first dose of vaccine

* Max dose: hRIG - 20IU/kg , eRIG - 40IU/kg body weight

* Vaccines should never be withheld regardless of the availability of RIG.

* Alternatives for RIG- WHO recommends monoclonal antibodies (mAb) as a 'cocktail' containing at least two antibodies against the rabies virus.

Administration of RIG:

* RIG should be administered into or around the wound site or sites.

* The remaining RIG, if any, should be injected IM at a site distant from the site of vaccine administration.

* RIG may be diluted to a volume sufficient for all wounds to be effectively and safely infiltrated.

Prioritization of RIG allocation (numbered according to priority order):

* Multiple bites

* Deep wounds

* Bites to head, neck, and hands

* Patients with severe immunodeficiency

* Confirmed/probable rabies in biting animal

* Bites, scratches, and exposure of mucous membranes caused by a bat

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP)

PrEP is considered in the following conditions:

* High-risk groups- laboratory staff, wildlife wardens, veterinarians, animal handlers, and travelers to endemic regions.

* Remote, rabies-endemic areas where access to PEP is difficult

* Areas where dog bite incidence is >5% per year

* Areas where vampire bat rabies is known to be present.

Pre-exposure rabies vaccination consists of two intramuscular (IM) or two intradermal (ID) doses. These are given on days 0 and 3.

* Adults - the vaccine should always be administered in the deltoid area of the arm

* Young children (under 1 year of age)- Administration into the anterolateral area of the thigh is recommended.

* Rabies vaccine should never be administered in the gluteal area. Administration in this manner will result in lower neutralizing antibody titers.

For exposed or re-exposed patients who can document previous completion of PEP the following guidelines would be applicable:

* Proper wound management should be done.

* There is no need for the administration of RIG.

* One site ID or IM vaccine administration on days 0 and 3.

Only adequate wound washing would be required in case of re-exposure where the animal bite victim has documented proof of complete PEP within the last three months.

The following cases are treated as fresh cases and given full PEP:

* Those who have previously received full post-exposure treatment with neural tissue vaccines (NTV) or vaccines of unproven potency

* Those who cannot document complete PEP or PrEP treatment
questions.learning: Wound cleaning+ rabies vaccine on day 0 & 3 — This patient should receive 2 doses of vaccine on days 0 & 3 as he has received a prior course of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) > 3 months ago.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct in respect of pulmonary involvement in rheumatoid disease?
options: Rheumatoid pulmonary nodules are usually asymptomatic and detected incidentally on imaging
Rheumatoid pulmonary nodules are often solitary and located near hilum
Pleural effusion in these patients is transudative and usually bilateral
Combination of pleural effusion and pneumoconiosis in these patients is known as Caplan syndrome
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rheumatoid pulmonary nodules are usually asymptomatic and detected incidentally on imaging

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic autoimmune disease with several extra-articular pulmonary manifestations, including interstitial lung disease (ILD), pleural disease, pulmonary nodules, airway disease, and pulmonary hypertension. Rheumatoid pulmonary nodules are usually:

• Asymptomatic
• Multiple
• Peripheral and subpleural
• Incidentally detected on chest X-ray or CT scan
• More common in seropositive RA, males, smokers, and patients with rheumatoid nodules elsewhere.

Why not the other options?

• B. Rheumatoid pulmonary nodules are often solitary and located near hilum: Incorrect. They are typically multiple, peripheral, and subpleural, not hilar.
• C. Pleural effusion is transudative and usually bilateral: Incorrect. Rheumatoid pleural effusions are exudative, usually unilateral, with low glucose, low pH, and high LDH. ⭐
• D. Combination of pleural effusion and pneumoconiosis is known as Caplan syndrome: Incorrect. Caplan syndrome is the combination of rheumatoid arthritis and pneumoconiosis (especially coal workers’ pneumoconiosis or silicosis) with multiple pulmonary nodules—not pleural effusion.
questions.learning: Rheumatoid pulmonary nodules are usually asymptomatic and detected incidentally on imaging Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic autoimmune disease with several extra-articular pulmonary manifestations, including interstitial lung disease (ILD), pleural…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following may be seen during clinical examination in a patient of Diabetes mellitus? 1. Necrobiosis lipoidica 2. Charcot neuroarthropathy 3. Exudative maculopathy 4. Acanthosis nigricans Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3 and 4

All four findings can be associated with diabetes mellitus.

• 1. Necrobiosis lipoidica: Correct.

• Strongly associated with diabetes, particularly type 1 DM.
• Presents as yellow-brown, atrophic plaques with prominent telangiectasia, usually on the shins.

• 2. Charcot neuroarthropathy: Correct.

• Occurs due to diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
• Repeated unrecognized trauma causes joint destruction, classically affecting the midfoot.
• The foot may become warm, swollen, and deformed.

• 3. Exudative maculopathy: Correct.

• A manifestation of diabetic retinopathy, particularly diabetic macular edema.
• Retinal leakage produces hard exudates, which may form a circinate pattern around the macula.

• 4. Acanthosis nigricans: Correct.

• Associated with insulin resistance, particularly in type 2 DM.
• Presents as hyperpigmented, velvety thickening of the skin, commonly in the neck and axillae.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 and 4 All four findings can be associated with diabetes mellitus. • 1. Necrobiosis lipoidica: Correct. • Strongly associated with diabetes, particularly type 1 DM. • Presents as yellow-brown, atrophic plaques with prominent telangiectasia, usually…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Aprepitant is a drug used in the treatment of some cases of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. NK1 antagonist

Key clue:

• Chemotherapy-induced nausea & vomiting (CINV)

Think of the “big 3 antiemetic pathways”:

1. Serotonin (5-HT3)
2. Dopamine (D2)
3.

Substance P (NK1)

4.

Aprepitant belongs to the Substance P pathway. Aprepitant = Neurokinin-1 (NK1) receptor antagonist

5. Blocks Substance P

Acts at:

• Vomiting center (medulla)
• Chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ)

Chemotherapy

↓

Enterochromaffin cells release serotonin

↓

5-HT3 activation → acute vomiting

+

Substance P release (brainstem)

↓

NK1 receptor activation → delayed vomiting

Aprepitant blocks NK1 receptors

↓

Prevents delayed phase vomiting

| Phase | Mediator | Drug

| ----- | -------- | ----

| Acute (0–24 hr) | Serotonin (5-HT3) | Ondansetron

| Delayed (>24 hr) | Substance P | Aprepitant

| Drug | Mechanism | Use

| ---- | --------- | ---

| Aprepitant | NK1 antagonist | CINV (delayed phase)

| Ondansetron | 5-HT3 antagonist | Acute vomiting

| Metoclopramide | D2 antagonist | General antiemetic

| Domperidone | Peripheral D2 blocker | GI motility
