questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 70-year-old man comes to the OPD due to increasing headaches, nausea, and vomiting. Medical history is significant for a transient ischemic attack that led to a right carotid endarterectomy 5 years ago. Blood pressure is 220/120 mm Hg and pulse is 70/min. Bilateral abdominal bruits are present. Blood testing in this patient would most likely show which of the following?
options: Low renin, low aldosterone, high angiotensin II, low potassium
High renin, high aldosterone, high angiotensin II, low potassium
Low renin, high aldosterone, high angiotensin II, low potassium
Low renin, low aldosterone, low angiotensin II, high potassium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High renin, high aldosterone, high angiotensin II, low potassium

Severe hypertension with bilateral abdominal bruits suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis, causing renovascular hypertension.

Renal hypoperfusion stimulates renin release, activating RAAS:

• ↑ Renin
• ↑ Angiotensin II
• ↑ Aldosterone → Na⁺ retention & K⁺ loss (hypokalemia)

Thus, renovascular hypertension is characterized by high renin, high angiotensin II, high aldosterone, and low potassium.
questions.learning: High renin, high aldosterone, high angiotensin II, low potassium Severe hypertension with bilateral abdominal bruits suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis, causing renovascular hypertension.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A registered medical practitioner is requested by a survivor of sexual violence to examine her. Within what time must the practitioner take a vaginal swab to look for the presence of spermatozoa?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Within 72 hours

A vaginal swab of a rape victim demonstrates spermatozoa if the vaginal swab is taken within 72 hours after an assault.

However, a vaginal swab can be taken within 96 hours to demonstrate semen.

Evidence on the outside of the body and on materials such as clothing can be collected even after 96 hours.
questions.learning: Within 72 hours — A vaginal swab of a rape victim demonstrates spermatozoa if the vaginal swab is taken within 72 hours after an assault. However, a vaginal swab can be taken within 96 hours to demonstrate semen.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Under the Stepwise Approach to the management of Bronchial Asthma, which one of the following is the correct initial treatment at Step 1 for a patient diagnosed with Asthma?
options: Low dose inhaled corticosteroid plus oral corticosteroid
Low dose inhaled corticosteroid plus long acting anti-muscarinic agents
Low dose inhaled corticosteroid plus leukotriene antagonist
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Low dose inhaled corticosteroid only

Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are the cornerstone of asthma management because asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways. Even patients with mild asthma have underlying airway inflammation, and early initiation of low-dose ICS reduces symptoms, improves lung function, decreases airway hyperresponsiveness, and significantly lowers the risk of severe exacerbations.

At Step 1, the recommended controller treatment is low-dose inhaled corticosteroids, which target the underlying airway inflammation and provide effective long-term disease control.

Why not the other options?

• B. Low-dose inhaled corticosteroid plus oral corticosteroid: Oral corticosteroids are reserved for acute severe exacerbations or difficult-to-control asthma, not initial therapy.
• C. Low-dose inhaled corticosteroid plus long-acting antimuscarinic agent (LAMA): LAMA (e.g., tiotropium) is an add-on therapy in severe asthma, not first-line treatment.
• D. Low-dose inhaled corticosteroid plus leukotriene antagonist: Leukotriene receptor antagonists (e.g., montelukast) are alternative or add-on therapies, not routine initial treatment.
questions.learning: Low dose inhaled corticosteroid only Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are the cornerstone of asthma management because asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is pneumomediastinum commonly found?
questions.explanation: Pneumomediastinum (air in the mediastinum) is a hallmark clinical and radiological finding in Boerhaave syndrome. As the esophagus ruptures during forceful vomiting, air is forced into the surrounding mediastinal space. This can lead to Mackler's triad: vomiting, chest pain, and subcutaneous emphysema. Mallory-Weiss syndrome (Option C) involves only a partial-thickness mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction, which causes hematemesis (vomiting blood) but does not result in perforation or pneumomediastinum. Pulsion diverticula (Option A), such as Zenker's diverticulum, are outpocketings of the mucosa that can cause dysphagia but rarely rupture into the mediastinum unless severely complicated. Pericarditis (Option D) is an inflammation of the heart's sac and does not involve air leakage. On examination, pneumomediastinum may produce "Hamman's crunch," a crunching sound heard over the heart synchronized with the heartbeat
questions.learning: Pneumomediastinum (air in the mediastinum) is a hallmark clinical and radiological finding in Boerhaave syndrome. As the esophagus ruptures during forceful vomiting, air is forced into the surrounding mediastinal space.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which statement correctly explains the mechanism of action of labetalol?
options: Directly acts as arterial vasodilator resulting in indirect effect tachycardia.
Blocks both alpha and beta-adrenergic receptors.
Primarily acts as a vasodilator with little effect on arterioles
Decreases peripheral vascular resistance by directly acting as a relaxant for vascular smooth muscles.
questions.explanation: Labetalol is a unique antihypertensive agent classified as a combined alpha- and beta-adrenergic antagonist. Specifically, it blocks both alpha-1 and non-selective beta ( and ) receptors. The -blockade causes systemic vasodilation, which lowers blood pressure by reducing peripheral vascular resistance. Simultaneously, its -blockade prevents the reflex tachycardia that would normally occur in response to a drop in blood pressure. This dual action makes it highly effective and safe. Option A describes pure vasodilators like hydralazine. Options C and D are inaccurate descriptions of its direct receptor-mediated effects. Labetalol is especially notable for its safety in managing hypertensive emergencies and is a first-line drug for treating hypertension during pregnancy (e.g., pre-eclampsia). It has a ratio of alpha-to-beta blockade of approximately 1:3 for oral dosing and 1:7 for intravenous use. Understanding this combined blockade is essential for utilizing labetalol correctly in clinical scenarios where both rapid pressure reduction and heart rate control are required
questions.learning: Labetalol is a unique antihypertensive agent classified as a combined alpha- and beta-adrenergic antagonist. Specifically, it blocks both alpha-1 and non-selective beta ( and ) receptors.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 32-year-old patient presents with a visible swelling just below the ear accompanied by pain in the earlobe. The patient also reports difficulty in completely closing the left eye and problems while eating. This combination of findings points toward involvement of a cranial nerve. Which nerve is most likely damaged based on this presentation?
questions.explanation: The patient’s inability to fully close the eye and difficulty eating (likely due to cheek muscle weakness) are classic signs of facial nerve (Cranial Nerve VII) palsy. The facial nerve passes through the parotid gland, located just beneath the ear. A swelling in this area, such as a parotid tumor or inflammation, can compress the nerve and result in paralysis of the muscles of facial expression, including the orbicularis oculi and buccinator. The greater auricular nerve (Option A) provides sensation to the earlobe and skin over the parotid but is not involved in eye closure or mastication movements. The auriculotemporal nerve (Option B) provides sensory innervation to the temple and ear but not motor control of the face. The vagus nerve (Option D) controls visceral functions and palate/throat muscles. Therefore, the combination of periauricular swelling and motor facial paralysis identifies the facial nerve as the site of injury
questions.learning: The patient’s inability to fully close the eye and difficulty eating (likely due to cheek muscle weakness) are classic signs of facial nerve (Cranial Nerve VII) palsy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old female presents with skin thickening, muscle weakness, and the peripheries becoming pale on exposure to cold. She is positive for ANA and anti-Scl-70 antibodies. Her creatinine kinase is elevated and muscle biopsy shows perifascicular infiltration. What is the antibody associated with this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anti-PM-Scl antibody

The given patient with a history and findings suggestive of diffuse systemic sclerosis and dermatomyositis/polymyositis is most likely to be suffering from overlap syndrome. The presence of skin thickening, Reynaud's phenomenon, and anti-Scl-70 antibodies are suggestive of diffuse systemic sclerosis, while muscle weakness and perifascicular infiltration are suggestive of dermatomyositis/polymyositis.

In overlap syndromes involving polymyositis/dermatomyositis and systemic sclerosis, anti-PM-Scl antibodies are found in close to 50% of the patients, while anti-Jo-1 antibodies were found to be positive in 20-30% of the patients.

Anti-centromere antibodies (option B) are seen in limited-cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Anti-U3-RNP antibodies (also known as anti-fibrillin antibodies) are seen in both limited-cutaneous and diffuse systemic sclerosis. They signify an increased risk of the patient developing pulmonary arterial hypertension, interstitial lung disease, scleroderma renal crisis, and myositis.
questions.learning: Anti-PM-Scl antibody — The given patient with a history and findings suggestive of diffuse systemic sclerosis and dermatomyositis/polymyositis is most likely to be suffering from overlap syndrome.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which anatomical plane, located between the rectus abdominis muscle and the transversalis fascia, contains the neurovascular structures that supply the abdominal wall?
options: Between the internal oblique and external oblique
Between the internal oblique and rectus abdominis
Between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis
questions.explanation: The abdominal wall is composed of several muscle layers, and the primary neurovascular structures (including the lower intercostal, subcostal, and iliohypogastric nerves) travel within a specific anatomical plane. This neurovascular plane is situated between the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis muscles. This is analogous to the intercostal space where the neurovascular bundle travels between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles. Option A (between internal and external oblique) and Option C (between internal oblique and rectus) do not house the primary nerve trunks. Option B (deep to transversus abdominis) refers to the preperitoneal space. Understanding this plane is clinically vital for surgeons when performing abdominal incisions or for anesthesiologists performing a TAP (Transversus Abdominis Plane) block, where local anesthetic is injected exactly into this space to provide regional analgesia. Therefore, the plane between the two deepest flat muscles of the abdomen is the correct anatomical answer
questions.learning: The abdominal wall is composed of several muscle layers, and the primary neurovascular structures (including the lower intercostal, subcostal, and iliohypogastric nerves) travel within a specific anatomical plane.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-day-old neonate was admitted to the NICU after he was observed to have movements as shown in the clip. His APGAR scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. His blood sugar was within the normal range in the first 24 hours. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Focal clonic seizure

The video clip of a 2-day-old neonate exhibiting repetitive, rhythmic movement in unilateral upper and lower limbs suggests a neonatal seizure of focal clonic type.

A focal clonic seizure is characterized by multiple, repetitive, rhythmic contractions of muscle groups of the limbs, face, or trunk, maybe unifocal or multifocal. It may occur synchronously or asynchronously in muscle groups on one side of the body. It may occur simultaneously but asynchronously on both sides. It cannot be suppressed by restraint.

Other options:

Option A: Focal tonic seizures are characterized by sustained posturing of a single limb, sustained asymmetrical posturing of the trunk, and sustained eye deviation. They cannot be provoked by stimulation or suppressed by restraint.

Option C: Spasms are sudden generalized jerks lasting 1-2 sec and are usually associated with a single, very brief, generalized discharge. They may be flexor, extensor, or mixed extensor/flexor and can occur in clusters. They too cannot be provoked by stimulation or suppressed by restraint.

Option D: Subtle seizures include transient eye deviations, nystagmus, blinking, mouthing, abnormal extremity movements (rowing, swimming, cycling, pedalling), fluctuations in heart rate, hypertension episodes, and apnea. They are more common in preterm than in term babies.

Myoclonic seizures are random, single, rapid muscle contractions of the limbs, face, or trunk. They are not repetitive or may recur at a slow rate. They can be generalized, focal, or fragmentary. They can be provoked by stimulation.

Clinically apparent seizures in a neonate should be treated if they last >3 minutes or are brief serial seizures. In all neonates with seizures, hypoglycemia, CNS infection, and hypocalcemia should be ruled out before starting anti-epileptic drug treatment.

Causes of neonatal seizure according to the age of presentation:

1 to 4 days
4 to 14 days
2 to 8 weeks

Hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy

Maternal use of narcotics or barbiturates

Drug toxicity: lidocaine, penicillin

Intraventricular hemorrhage

Hypocalcemia, sepsis, hypoglycemia, hypomagnesemia,  hypo or hypernatremia

Galactosemia, urea cycle disorders

Meningitis (bacterial)

Encephalitis (enteroviral, herpes simplex)

Hypocalcemia, hypoglycemia

Galactosemia, fructosemia,

Hyperinsulinism, hyperammonemia syndrome

Herpes simplex or enteroviral encephalitis, bacterial meningitis

Subdural hematoma, child abuse

Aminoaciduria, urea cycle defects

Malformations of cortical development

Tuberous sclerosis

Sturge-Weber syndrome
questions.learning: Focal clonic seizure — The video clip of a 2-day-old neonate exhibiting repetitive, rhythmic movement in unilateral upper and lower limbs suggests a neonatal seizure of focal clonic type.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: All of the following are contraceptive methods used post-coitus except: (NEET PG 2020)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Danazol

Emergency contraception (postcoital contraception) is used to prevent pregnancy after unprotected intercourse.

Methods used for emergency contraception include:

• High-dose combined estrogen-progestin pills (Yuzpe method)
• Levonorgestrel pills
• Mifepristone (RU-486)
• Copper IUCD (CuT 200/CuT 380A)

Copper IUCD is one of the most effective methods when inserted within 5 days of unprotected intercourse. Danazol is not used for emergency contraception. It is a synthetic androgen primarily used for:

• Endometriosis
• Fibrocystic breast disease
• Hereditary angioedema

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Normal diameter of artery to vein at the optic disc margin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2:3

The normal diameter ratio of the central retinal artery to the central retinal vein at the optic disc margin is 2:3.

The ratio 2:3 means that the artery’s diameter is approximately two-thirds of the vein’s diameter. This is considered the physiological normal. The ratio is assessed during the fundoscopic examination, and significant deviations can indicate pathological conditions:

• Decreased ratio (arteriolar narrowing) may suggest hypertension or arteriosclerosis.
• Increased ratio (relative venous narrowing) is less common but may occur in rare conditions.
questions.learning: 2:3 The normal diameter ratio of the central retinal artery to the central retinal vein at the optic disc margin is 2:3. The ratio 2:3 means that the artery’s diameter is approximately two-thirds of the vein’s diameter.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 39-year-old male patient presented with complaints of fever and cough. His chest radiograph shows air bronchogram sign. The probable diagnosis is :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Consolidation

The radiograph shows air bronchogram sign in a lung with consolidation, seen in pneumonia, which is supported by the clinical history of this patient.

An air bronchogram is a tubular outline of an airway made visible when there is filling of the surrounding alveoli by fluid or inflammatory exudates.

The causes of air bronchogram are as follows:

• Lung consolidation
• Pulmonary edema
• Nonobstructive pulmonary atelectasis
• Severe interstitial disease
• Neoplasm
• Normal expiration

Pleural effusion is seen as a homogenous opacity on chest radiograph.

The given radiograph shows peribronchial thickening and air bronchogram sign:
questions.learning: Consolidation — The radiograph shows air bronchogram sign in a lung with consolidation, seen in pneumonia, which is supported by the clinical history of this patient.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A group of 20 friends kept partying till late at night. Two of them ate pastries from outside. They present with nausea and vomiting in the early morning. What is the most likely causative agent implicated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Enterotoxin of Staphylococcus

The most likely causative agent in the given scenario is enterotoxin of Staphylococcus aureus. It causes food poisoning within 30 minutes to 6 hours after consumption of the contaminated food.

The common sources of infection are the foods that are not cooked after handling. These include sliced meats, puddings, pastries, and sandwiches. Patients present with nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, and diarrhea.

Food poisoning is caused by enterotoxin produced by S. aureus. It is a preformed toxin that is relatively heat stable while most of the other exotoxins are heat-labile. It stimulates the vagus nerve and vomiting center of the brain and also stimulates intestinal peristaltic activity. Eight antigenic types of enterotoxin are currently known of which Type  A toxin is responsible for most cases.

Other options:

Option B: Food poisoning after consumption of fried rice or chinese street food is strongly suggestive of Bacillus cereus (Serotypes 1, 3, 5). Two mechanisms of action have been described for the enterotoxin of B.cereus, one involving stimulation of the cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) system and the other independent of it.

Food poisoning after eating food contaminated with Bacillus cereus is of two types, namely diarrheal type and emetic type, caused by an enterotoxin and an emetic toxin respectively.

Option D: Shiga toxin acts by inactivating 60s ribosomal subunit thereby inhibiting protein synthesis. Shigella dysenteriae causes acute onset of symptoms(fever, abdominal cramps) with dysentery and tenesmus. It also gives a positive Sereny test and is non-lactose fermenting.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient with multiple colonic polyps is diagnosed with colorectal carcinoma and has a strong family history suggestive of Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC). Which DNA repair mechanism is most likely defective in this condition?
questions.explanation: Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC), also known as Lynch syndrome, is caused by a defect in the DNA mismatch repair (MMR) system. Mutations in genes like hMSH2 (the most common) or hMSH1 prevent the correction of base-pairing errors during replication, leading to microsatellite instability and a high risk of malignancy. Nucleotide excision repair (Option A) fixes bulky lesions like those from UV radiation and is defective in xeroderma pigmentosum. Base excision repair (Option C) corrects small, non-bulky lesions caused by oxidation. Double-strand break repair (Option D) handles major chromosomal breaks and is linked to conditions like Ataxia-Telangiectasia or BRCA mutations. Because HNPCC is the specific diagnostic entity described, the mismatch repair pathway is the definitive biochemical defect. This highlights the importance of genetic screening for patients with early-onset colorectal cancers and significant family histories

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A new test was developed for detection of COVID-19. What is the sensitivity of the test as per the information provided above?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 37.5%

Sensitivity is the ability of a diagnostic test to correctly identify individuals who truly have the disease (true positives). It answers the question:

“Among those who have the disease, how many test positive?”

Formula:

• Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN) × 100

Where:

• TP (True Positive) = 60
• FN (False Negative) = 100

Calculation:

Sensitivity = 60 / (60 + 100) × 100

= 60 / 160 × 100

= 37.5%

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient underwent LASIK for myopia and now is undergoing cataract surgery. What is the formula used for lens power calculation in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Haigis L

Among the given options, the Haigis-L regression formula is used for calculating the lens power in a patient who is undergoing cataract surgery with a previous history of refractive surgery.

Haigis formula uses Axial Length (L), Corneal curvature (K), and Anterior Chamber Depth (ACD) for the calculation of IOL power (biometry).

• Keratometry measures the curvature of the anterior corneal surface.
• A-scan ultrasonography is used to determine the axial length.

Standard IOL calculations are unsuitable in any type of corneal refractive surgery as they are likely to result in residual refractive errors even after IOL implantation in these patients. In these patients, several other methods of calculating corneal refractive power are used which are then added to the standard and specific formulas such as the Masket, modified masket, Haigis L formula, and double-K method.

Other options:

Options A and B: SRK 1 and SRK 2 are the basic formulas used for IOL power calculations.

SRK formula: P = A-2.5L-0.9K where P is the power of IOL, A is a constant for the lens, L is the axial length and K is corneal curvature.

Option C: Hoffer Q formula is used for IOL power calculation in short eyes (hypermetropia). It uses only two variables; Axial length (L) and corneal curvature (K).
questions.learning: Haigis L Among the given options, the Haigis-L regression formula is used for calculating the lens power in a patient who is undergoing cataract surgery with a previous history of refractive surgery.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the cardiac muscle, the inhibition of Na+K+ATPase results in __?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Depolarisation

The inhibition of Na+K+-ATPase results in depolarisation.

An energy (ATP)-dependent pump system (Na+/K+-ATPase), is located on the sarcolemma, which pumps Na+ out and K+ into the cell.The Na+/K+-ATPase pump is electrogenic because it extrudes three Na+ for every two K+ entering the cell. By pumping more positive charges out of the cell than into it, the pump creates a negative potential within the cell. This electrogenic potential may be up to −10 mV.

If this pump stops working (such as when ATP is lost under hypoxic conditions), or if the activity of the pump is inhibited by cardiac glycosides such as digoxin, Na+ accumulates within the cell and intracellular K+ falls,resulting in a less negative (more depolarized) resting membrane potential.

Inhibition of this pump, therefore, causes depolarization resulting from changes in Na+ and K+ concentration gradients and from the loss of an electrogenic component of the membrane potential.

Action potential of myocardium:

* Phase 0: Depolarisation: Influx of Na+ into myocyte.

* Phase 1: Early repolarization: Efflux of K+ from myocyte.

* Phase 2: Plateau: Ca2+ enters myocardial cells via voltage regulated L-type Ca2+ channels.

* Phase 3: Repolarisation: Efflux of K+.

* Phase 4: Restoration of RMP: Restoration of Na+ and K+ by Na-K ATPase.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young woman with a past history of spontaneous abortion now presents with amenorrhea. Her serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) level is 6 mIU/mL. Based on her clinical history and hormonal findings, what is the most likely cause of her amenorrhea?
questions.explanation: Asherman syndrome refers to the presence of intrauterine adhesions (synechiae), most commonly following a vigorous dilation and curettage (D&C) performed for a spontaneous abortion. The adhesions obliterate the uterine cavity, leading to secondary amenorrhea despite normal hormonal function. The provided FSH level of 6 mIU/ml is within the "normal" range (typically 5–20 mIU/ml), which indicates that the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis is intact. Sheehan's syndrome (Option A) involves pituitary infarction after postpartum hemorrhage and would show "low" gonadotropins. Premature ovarian failure (Option B) would be characterized by a "very high" FSH (usually >40 mIU/ml) as the ovaries fail to respond. PCOS (Option C) typically presents with irregular periods and metabolic signs, not sudden amenorrhea following a procedure, and usually shows a high LH:FSH ratio. The clinical history of a procedure followed by amenorrhea with a normal FSH is pathognomonic for an "outflow tract" obstruction like Asherman syndrome. Diagnosis is confirmed by hysteroscopy
questions.learning: Asherman syndrome refers to the presence of intrauterine adhesions (synechiae), most commonly following a vigorous dilation and curettage (D&C) performed for a spontaneous abortion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: When performing diagnostic paracentesis in a patient with ascites using the midline approach, which needle gauge is commonly used for aspiration of the fluid?
questions.explanation: Paracentesis is a procedure used to sample or drain ascitic fluid from the peritoneal cavity. For a "diagnostic" paracentesis, where only a small amount of fluid (typically 20–50 ml) is needed for laboratory analysis (e.g., cell count, albumin, culture), a smaller needle is preferred to minimize trauma and the risk of a persistent leak or hematoma. A 22-gauge needle is typically used for this purpose. Larger bore needles, such as 14-gauge (Option A) or 16-gauge (Option B), are reserved for "therapeutic" paracentesis, where several liters of fluid are drained quickly to relieve symptoms of tension. A 17-gauge needle (Option C) is also unnecessarily large for simple diagnostics. The midline approach, usually 2 cm below the umbilicus along the linea alba, is chosen because it is relatively avascular. Using a fine-gauge needle ensures the procedure is safe and well-tolerated by the patient, while still allowing for the aspiration of fluid for essential diagnostic testing

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which intestinal disorder is commonly associated with dermatitis herpetiformis?
questions.explanation: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is a chronic, intensely pruritic, blistering skin condition that is considered the cutaneous manifestation of Celiac disease. Nearly all patients with DH have some degree of gluten-sensitive enteropathy (celiac disease), even if they do not have overt gastrointestinal symptoms. DH is characterized by symmetric, herpetiform (grouped) vesicles on extensor surfaces like the elbows and knees. Ulcerative colitis (Option A) and Crohn's disease (Option D) are forms of inflammatory bowel disease associated with other skin conditions like pyoderma gangrenosum or erythema nodosum, but not DH. Whipple's disease (Option B) is a rare systemic infection that causes malabsorption but is not associated with this specific skin disorder. The diagnosis of DH is confirmed by skin biopsy showing granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae. The primary treatment for both the skin and intestinal symptoms is a lifelong, strict gluten-free diet
questions.learning: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is a chronic, intensely pruritic, blistering skin condition that is considered the cutaneous manifestation of Celiac disease.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: On your morning walk in the park, you notice an unconscious man lying on the ground. Which of the following options would be the next best step?
options: Check carotid pulse, start CPR, and call for help; Defibrillate if no pulse.
Call for help, check pulse, do CPR, defibrillate if no pulse
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Call for help, check pulse, do CPR, defibrillate if no pulse

The next best step is to Call for help, check pulse, do CPR, defibrillate If no pulse.

Steps in basic life support:

First step – Assess safety of the surroundings.

Second step - Assess for responsiveness

Third step – Proceed if the patient is unresponsive. Shout for help.

If the patient is unresponsive, assess for breathing and carotid pulse simultaneously for no more than 10 seconds.

In the given scenario, it is already mentioned that you are in a park (scene safety has been assessed), and that the person is unconscious (responsiveness has been assessed). So, the immediate next step is to call for help, and start CPR.
questions.learning: Call for help, check pulse, do CPR, defibrillate if no pulse The next best step is to Call for help, check pulse, do CPR, defibrillate If no pulse. Steps in basic life support: First step – Assess safety of the surroundings.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A primigravida woman gives birth to a baby with the following defect. Identify the anomaly.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Open neural tube defect

The above clinical scenario, along with the image showing anencephaly and a contiguous bony defect of the spine, is suggestive of craniorachischisis which is an open neural tube defect that occurs due to failure of complete closure of the neural tube.

Craniorachischisis is a severe neural tube defect characterized by the failure of neural tube closure, resulting in the exposure of both the brain (anencephaly) and spinal cord (rachischisis). This condition leads to a completely open brain and spinal column, making it incompatible with life. The exposed neural tissues often become necrotic. It occurs due to defects in primary neurulation during early embryonic development.

The image given below shows craniorachischisis.

Other options:

Spina bifida is a general term used for neural tube defects affecting the spinal region and associated with splitting of the vertebral arches. It is characterized by gaps in the vertebral arches and may or may not involve the underlying neural tissue.

The illustration shown below shows spina bifida.

The 3 main types of spina bifida:

* Spina bifida occulta (Option C) is the mildest form of spina bifida. The skin covers the defect in the vertebral arches. The splits in the vertebrae are so small that the spinal cord does not protrude. The skin at the site of the lesion may be normal, or it may have some hair growing from it.

* Meningocele - The defect in the vertebra allows the meninges to protrude through the defect.

* Meningomyelocele (Option A) - A defect in the vertebral column allows the spinal cord with the meningeal coverings to protrude.

The image given below shows the different types of spina bifida.

Option D: Encephalocele is caused due to defects in the skull through which the meninges and/or neural tissue herniate. The squamous part of the occipital bone is the most frequently affected bone.

The image shows a newborn with encephalocele.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A body brought for autopsy is cold to touch, shows rigor mortis in all four limbs, and has fixed livor mortis on the back, with no evidence of putrefaction. Based on these findings, what is the estimated time since death?
questions.explanation: 12-24 hours The estimation of the postmortem interval (PMI) relies on the combined findings of algor, rigor, and livor mortis. In this case, the body is cold to the touch, suggesting death occurred more than 8–12 hours ago. Rigor mortis is fully established in all four limbs, a state that typically occurs around 12 hours post-death and lasts up to 24 hours. Livor mortis (postmortem staining) is fixed at the back, which usually indicates a fixation time of 6–12 hours. Most importantly, there are no signs of putrefaction; putrefaction generally begins only after 24–36 hours depending on environmental conditions. Combining these markers, the most accurate estimate for the time since death is 12–24 hours. Option B (6–12 hrs) is less likely because rigor would not be fully established in all limbs. Options C and D are incorrect because putrefaction would likely have started.
questions.learning: 12-24 hours The estimation of the postmortem interval (PMI) relies on the combined findings of algor, rigor, and livor mortis. In this case, the body is cold to the touch, suggesting death occurred more than 8–12 hours ago.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: You are a doctor in a village. A 1 yr old child who is not taking feeds, presents with fever and cough for 2 days. On examination, he is calm, with a respiratory rate of 51 breaths/min, and stridor is present. According to IMNCI (Integrated management of neonatal and childhood illnesses), how is he classified?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Severe Pneumonia

This child is classified as having a very severe disease/severe pneumonia.

Signs of very severe disease are:

* Stridor in a calm child

* Not able to drink

* Convulsions

* Abnormally sleepy or difficult to wake

* Severe malnutrition.

In any of these cases, an urgent referral is very important.
questions.learning: Severe Pneumonia — This child is classified as having a very severe disease/severe pneumonia. Signs of very severe disease are: * Stridor in a calm child * Not able to drink * Convulsions * Abnormally sleepy or difficult to wake * Severe malnutrition.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 13-year-old boy presents with involuntary dancing movements of his right hand. He was diagnosed with rheumatic fever. What constitutes the ganglia involved in the presenting complication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Caudate nucleus and putamen

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Sydenham's chorea, a complication of rheumatic fever. The choreic movements are caused by the destruction of D2 neurons of the striatum. The neostriatum consists of the caudate nucleus and putamen.

The image given below shows Sydenham's chorea in a patient.

Nomenclature of basal ganglia:

• Corpus striatum: Caudate nucleus + putamen+ globus pallidus
• Lentiform nucleus: Putamen + globus pallidus
• Neostriatum: Caudate nucleus + putamen

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a hospital, a healthcare worker is responsible for segregating biomedical waste according to standard waste management guidelines. As per these guidelines, which category of biomedical waste should be disposed of in a white (translucent) bag?
questions.explanation: According to the current Biomedical Waste Management Rules, the white disposal bag is specifically reserved for sharp waste. This includes needles, syringes with fixed needles, scalpel blades, and lancets. These containers must be puncture-proof and leak-proof to prevent accidental needle-stick injuries to healthcare personnel. Anatomical waste (Option A), such as tissues or body parts, must be placed in yellow bags for incineration. Glassware (Option C), including vials or broken glass, should be placed in blue-labeled containers or boxes. Plastic waste (Option D) like catheters, IV tubes, and gloves is typically disposed of in red bags for autoclaving or chemical treatment before recycling. Proper segregation is vital to ensure that sharps, which pose a high risk for transmitting bloodborne pathogens like HIV, are handled with specific sterilization protocols. Consequently, the healthcare worker must place all sharp items into the designated white container
questions.learning: According to the current Biomedical Waste Management Rules, the white disposal bag is specifically reserved for sharp waste. This includes needles, syringes with fixed needles, scalpel blades, and lancets.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 2-year-old child presents with a fever and lymphadenopathy. On an H&E stain, a biopsy reveals hallmark cells. An anaplastic large cell lymphoma diagnosis is made. Which translocation is most likely to occur?

Correct answer: D. t(2:5)

Anaplastic large cell lymphoma is frequently associated with the t(2;5) (p23;q35). The biopsy shows characteristic large anaplastic cells, some containing horseshoe-shaped nuclei and voluminous cytoplasm called hallmark cells.

It is a type of T-cell lymphoma that consists of large lymphoid cells. This occurs due to rearrangements in the ALK gene and usually affects children and young adults. It frequently involves soft tissue and carries a good prognosis. T-cell lymphomas with similar morphology without ALK positivity occur in older adults and have a bad prognosis. The genetic defect is found on chromosome 2p23 that results in the production of anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) with tyrosine kinase activity.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A renal biopsy of a patient is shown below. Identify the cell marked in the given histological image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Macula Densa

The structure in the histological image is the macula densa cells in the distal convoluted tubule.

Specialized cells at the start of the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) form the macula densa. They detect sodium and chloride concentrations of the fluid in the tubule (chemoreceptor). In response to elevated sodium and chloride, the macula densa cells trigger the contraction of the afferent arteriole, reducing the flow of blood to the glomerulus and the glomerular filtration rate.

This happens as follows: When there is increased sodium, there is increased sodium-potassium ATPase activity which leads to increased ATP hydrolysis causing more adenosine formation. The adenosine receptors on the macula densa cells stimulate it to release more calcium, so that there is vasoconstriction of the afferent arteriole, thereby decreasing the GFR.

Other options:

The given image constitutes the juxtaglomerular apparatus and has the following parts:

Option B: Lacis cells: Extraglomerular mesangial cells situated between afferent and efferent arteriole.

Option C: Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells: Modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole, they secrete renin. Fall in pressure in afferent arteriole stimulates renin release (mechanoreceptor), which, in turn, increases blood pressure.

Option D:  Glomerulus is a rounded tuft of anastomosing capillaries. The glomerular capillary wall is the filtering membrane and consists of fenestrated endothelial cells, basement membrane, and visceral epithelial cells called podocytes, which contain foot processes (pedicels) as shown below.
questions.learning: Macula Densa — The structure in the histological image is the macula densa cells in the distal convoluted tubule. Specialized cells at the start of the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) form the macula densa.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A person presented with a history of road traffic accident (RTA) and a crush wound in the thigh. He came to the doctor the next day. On examination, the wound appeared black with crepitus. What is the most likely organism involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Clostridium perfringens

The given clinical scenario of a present with blackish colored wound with crepitus following a extensive wound injury (crush injury) is highly suggestive of gas gangrene/ clostridial myonecrosis, which is caused by Clostridium perfringens.

Military wounds and trauma which cause extensive tissue damage provide an ideal environment for gas gangrene. C.perfringens is gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-bearing bacilli present in nature, especially in soil and faeces. Patients who are immunocompromised, diabetic, or have malignant disease are also at greater risk. The usual incubation period is <24 hours of injury.

Gas gangrene wound infections are associated with severe local wound pain and crepitus (gas in the tissues). The wound produces a thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate, in which Gram staining will reveal bacteria. Edema and spreading gangrene occur due to the release of collagenase, hyaluronidase, other proteases, and alpha-toxin. Early systemic complications like circulatory collapse and organ failure can occur without adequate treatment.

Management includes high doses of intravenous penicillin and aggressive debridement of affected tissues. Amputations should be performed under antibiotic prophylaxis.

Other options:

Option A: C. tetani is an anaerobic, terminal spore-bearing, Gram-positive bacterium. It causes tetanus following implantation into tissues or a wound, and it usually presents with spasms.

Option B: C. difficile, a gram-positive anaerobic bacillus, causes Clostridioides (formerly Clostridium) difficile infection (CDI) after ingestion of spores of the organism. The more severe form of the condition is known as pseudomembranous colitis (PMC). It is most commonly associated with prolonged antimicrobial use which interferes with the commensal colonic microflora. The most commonly implicated antibiotics are cephalosporins, ampicillin, and clindamycin.

Option C: C. botulinum causes botulism, a paralytic disease that usually presents as a form of food poisoning.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the main source of reducing equivalents required for fatty acid synthesis in the liver?
questions.explanation: Fatty acid synthesis is an endergonic, reductive process that requires a significant supply of NADPH as a reducing equivalent. The Hexose Monophosphate (HMP) shunt pathway, also known as the Pentose Phosphate Pathway, is the primary source of this NADPH in the liver. Specifically, the oxidative phase of the HMP shunt, catalyzed by glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, generates the NADPH used by the fatty acid synthase complex. Glycolysis (Option B) and the Tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle (Option C) primarily produce NADH, which is used for ATP generation in the electron transport chain rather than reductive biosynthesis. The uronic acid pathway (Option D) is involved in the synthesis of glucuronic acid and does not provide major reducing equivalents for lipogenesis. Therefore, the liver's capacity for fat synthesis is directly dependent on the activity of the HMP shunt

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida in labor at 5 cm cervical dilatation suddenly develops severe fetal bradycardia. On vaginal examination, cord prolapse is detected and the cord is still pulsating. What should be the immediate next step in management?
options: Fill the bladder and put back the cord
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trendelenburg, push the head up

Cord prolapse occurs when the umbilical cord descends before the fetal presenting part, leading to cord compression and fetal hypoxia. Immediate Action Is Needed. Cord compression leads to:

Cord compression

↓

Reduced fetal oxygen supply

↓

Fetal bradycardia

↓

Fetal hypoxia

↓

Risk of fetal death

Therefore immediate decompression of the cord is essential.

Initial emergency measures include:

| Step | Purpose

| ---- | -------

| Trendelenburg or knee-chest position | Reduce cord compression

| Manual elevation of presenting part | Relieve pressure on cord

| Avoid handling the cord | Prevent vasospasm

| Oxygen to mother | Improve fetal oxygenation

After stabilization: Emergency cesarean section is performed.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child visited the hospital with her mother with complaints of severe fatigue, lethargy, pallor and irritation. She is a known case of iron deficiency anaemia (IDA) and is on oral iron supplements. On reviewing the child, the physician in charge plans to start IV iron supplementation. What is the next best test to be done in assessing this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Serum ferritin

Assessing serum ferritin is the next best step in this diagnosed case of iron deficiency anaemia (IDA).

The reference standard to diagnose and monitor IDA is serum ferritin level. A decrease in the same is the earliest sign of IDA.

Since it is expensive and not widely available, an inexpensive & simpler way of evaluation is the Mentzer index.

The progression to iron deficiency develops in 3 stages:

* Stage of negative iron balance - Decrease in iron stores with normal serum iron and RBC morphology

* Stage of iron-deficient erythropoiesis - Decrease in serum iron levels with normal RBC morphology

* Stage of iron deficiency anaemia - Microcytic hypochromic RBCs.
questions.learning: Serum ferritin Assessing serum ferritin is the next best step in this diagnosed case of iron deficiency anaemia (IDA). The reference standard to diagnose and monitor IDA is serum ferritin level.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly male patient presents with persistent fatigue and anemia. Given his clinical profile, what is the recommended screening protocol for colon cancer in this patient?
options: Fecal occult blood testing every 2 years
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Colonoscopy every 10 years

Anemia and fatigue in an elderly patient can be indicative of gastrointestinal bleeding, possibly from colorectal cancer, the most appropriate protocol for screening for colon cancer is a colonoscopy every 10 years.

Current ACS guidelines advocate screening the average-risk population for colorectal carcinoma beginning at age 50 years. Screening recommendations include the following:

* Annual faecal occult blood test (FOBT), or

* Flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, or

* FOBT and flexible sigmoidoscopy in combination every 5 years, or

* Air-contrast barium enema every 5 years, or

* Colonoscopy every 10 years.

A positive FOBT should be followed by a colonoscopy.

Patients with other risk factors (considered a high-risk population) should be screened earlier and more frequently, as shown below:

Population
Initial age
Recommendation

Familial colorectal cancer first-degree relative
40 years of age or 10 years before the age of the youngest affected relative (whichever is earlier)
Colonoscopy every 5 years

Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis)
At diagnosis; then 8 years after diagnosis
Colonoscopy with multiple biopsies every 1–2 years

Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)
10–12 years of age
Annual flexible sigmoidoscopy

Lynch syndrome (HNPCC)
20–25 years of age
Colonoscopy every 1–2 years

For individuals at average risk of colon cancer, current guidelines recommend colonoscopy as the gold standard for screening. Colonoscopy allows direct visualization of the entire colon and is effective at detecting both polyps and cancers. Given the patient's age, symptoms of anemia, and potential risk factors, a colonoscopy every 10 years is an appropriate protocol for colorectal cancer screening.
questions.learning: Colonoscopy every 10 years Anemia and fatigue in an elderly patient can be indicative of gastrointestinal bleeding, possibly from colorectal cancer, the most appropriate protocol for screening for colon cancer is a colonoscopy every 10 years.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Sulfasalazine is commonly used in the treatment of ulcerative colitis and rheumatoid arthritis. Which of the following are recognized adverse effects of sulfasalazine? A. Bone marrow suppression causing leukopenia B. Stevens–Johnson syndrome C. Reversible oligospermia D. Ototoxicity E. Hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency patient F. Macrocytic anemia G. Pneumonitis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. All except D

Sulfasalazine, a 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) derivative, is used in ulcerative colitis and rheumatoid arthritis and has several recognized adverse effects.

Important adverse effects include:

• Bone marrow suppression → leukopenia
• Stevens–Johnson syndrome (rare hypersensitivity reaction)
• Reversible oligospermia (affects sperm motility and count)
• Hemolytic anemia, especially in G6PD deficiency
• Folate deficiency leading to macrocytic anemia
• Hypersensitivity reactions including pneumonitis

Not associated: Ototoxicity (seen with drugs like aminoglycosides or loop diuretics).
questions.learning: All except D Sulfasalazine, a 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) derivative, is used in ulcerative colitis and rheumatoid arthritis and has several recognized adverse effects.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 2-month-old male infant presents with scrotal swelling that has been present since birth. Now the swelling has become suddenly painful, red, and irreducible. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Strangulated inguinal hernia

In infants, inguinal hernias occur due to a persistent patent processus vaginalis.

Normally the processus vaginalis closes after birth.

• If it remains open, Abdominal contents (usually intestine) can herniate into the inguinal canal and scrotum.
• When the herniated bowel becomes trapped and its blood supply is compromised, it leads to→ Strangulated inguinal hernia

Typical features include:

• Pain
• Redness
• Irreducible swelling
• Infant irritability or vomiting

A) Acute epididymo-orchitis

• rare in infants
• Usually occurs in adolescents or adults
• Presents with fever and gradual pain, not swelling since birth.

B) Testicular torsion

Occurs mainly in:

• Neonates
• Adolescents

But it does not present as a swelling present since birth.

D) Hydrocele

Hydrocele features:

• Painless swelling
• Transilluminant
• Usually soft and reducible or fluctuant
• Not red or acutely painful

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 39-year-old woman is brought to the psychiatry clinic by her daughter because of excessive accumulation of household items over the past several years. The patient says she feels extremely distressed whenever she tries to throw away old newspapers, clothes, or broken utensils, believing they might be useful in the future. As a result, most rooms in her house are cluttered, making them difficult to use. She has attempted to declutter several times but becomes overwhelmingly anxious and stops. She has no symptoms of depression, psychosis, or obsessive intrusive thoughts. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?
options: Assistance in sorting and discarding her possessions
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cognitive-behavioral therapy

This patient has hoarding disorder, characterized by:

• Persistent difficulty discarding possessions
• Distress when attempting to discard items
• Clutter severe enough to impair normal use of living spaces

CBT specifically designed for hoarding disorder is the first-line treatment, focusing on organization skills, cognitive restructuring, and gradual exposure to discarding possessions.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Assistance in sorting/discarding her possessions: May worsen anxiety unless done as part of a structured CBT program.
• B. Clomipramine: Used mainly for OCD; not first-line for hoarding disorder.
• C. Clonazepam: Relieves anxiety temporarily but does not treat hoarding behavior.
• Psychodynamic psychotherapy: Limited evidence of benefit.
• Quetiapine: No established role in primary hoarding disorder.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alcohol

Alcohol consumption is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis, accounting for 60–70% of the cases. Smoking increases the risk of alcohol-induced chronic pancreatitis.

Cystic fibrosis is the most common cause of chronic pancreatitis in the pediatric age group.

Other causes of chronic pancreatitis include:

• Pancreatic divisum
• Annular pancreas
• Hyperlipidemia
• Hypercalcemia
• Hyperparathyroidism
• Chronic duct obstruction
• Autoimmune pancreatitis
• Cystic fibrosis
• Tropical pancreatitis
• Hereditary pancreatitis

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young girl presents with menstrual irregularity, acne, increased hair growth with a Ferriman Gallway score of 8, and a BMI of 29. Her mother has diabetes. Which is not a management option?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. OCP + Anti androgen

These features strongly suggest Polycystic Ovary Syndrome. Anti-androgens are not first-line therapy initially and are usually added only if hirsutism persists after OCP therapy.

First-line therapy is OCP alone. Anti-androgens are added only if symptoms persist after ≥6 months. Lifestyle modification and metabolic counselling are essential in PCOS.

PCOS is a common endocrine disorder characterized by:

| Feature | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Menstrual irregularity | Anovulation

| Hyperandrogenism | Acne, hirsutism

| Obesity | Insulin resistance

Diagnosis is based on Rotterdam criteria (any 2 of 3):

1. Oligo/anovulation
2. Hyperandrogenism
3. Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound

The Ferriman–Gallwey score assesses hirsutism.

| Score | Interpretation

| ----- | --------------

| <8 | Normal

| ≥8 | Hirsutism

This patient has mild hirsutism.

Treatment depends on symptoms and metabolic risk.

First-line management

| Treatment | Purpose

| --------- | -------

| Lifestyle modification | Weight reduction

| Exercise / yoga | Improves insulin resistance

| Combined oral contraceptive pills (OCP) | Regulate cycles and reduce androgen

Thus options A, C, and D are correct management options.
questions.learning: OCP + Anti androgen — These features strongly suggest Polycystic Ovary Syndrome. Anti-androgens are not first-line therapy initially and are usually added only if hirsutism persists after OCP therapy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: For a woman with a prior pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect, what is the recommended folic acid dosage when planning conception?
questions.explanation: The standard periconceptional dose of folic acid for healthy women is 400 mcg (0.4 mg) daily to prevent neural tube defects (NTDs) (Option A). However, for a woman with a high risk—specifically those with a history of a previous pregnancy complicated by an NTD—clinical guidelines mandate a significantly higher dose. The recommended dosage for these women is 4 mg/day (Option D), which is ten times the standard dose . This high-dose supplementation should begin at least one month (ideally three) before conception and continue through the first trimester. Options B (1 mg) and C (2 mg) are insufficient based on international safety standards for secondary prevention. This intervention is proven to reduce the risk of NTD recurrence by over 70%. Therefore, for a woman with a prior affected pregnancy, 4 mg is the definitive and life-saving dosage recommendation

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the finding associated with the condition shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Isomorphic phenomenon

The image shows plaque psoriasis of the dorsum of the hand, and isomorphic or Koebner phenomenon is associated with the condition.

Option B: Meyerson phenomenon refers to the formation of an eczematous ring around a melanocytic nevus.

Option C: Gottron's papules are violaceous, erythematous papules overlying the dorsal interphalangeal or metacarpophalangeal, elbow, or knee joints.

Option D: Nikolsky sign refers to easy peeling of skin on applying tangential pressure over a bony prominence and is classically seen in pemphigus and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presented with fever and abdominal pain. Investigations showed the given findings. Which of the following statements is true regarding this condition?
options: Angioembolization is the treatment of choice
Echinococcus species is involved in Etiology
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Echinococcus species is involved in Etiology

This image shows a Hydatid cyst, most commonly caused by Echinococcus granulosus.

The Ultrasound/CT shows classic hydatid features:

• Cyst with internal floating membrane (“water-lily sign”).
• Daughter cysts inside the main cyst.
• Typically occurs in the liver.

Clinical clues in the question: Fever /Abdominal pain/ Cystic liver lesion with floating membrane.

Life cycle:

• Dog = definitive host
• Sheep = intermediate host
• Humans = accidental host

Humans ingest eggs → larvae reach liver via portal circulation → form hydatid cysts.

A) Surgery is mandatory ❌

Surgery is not always required. Management include:

• Albendazole
• PAIR technique

PAIR = Puncture ; Aspiration; Injection of scolicidal agent;  Reaspiration

Surgery is done only if:

• cyst is very large
• complicated
• ruptured
• PAIR not feasible

B) Fine needle aspiration cytology is diagnostic ❌

FNAC is contraindicated.

Why? If the cyst is punctured accidentally:

• Anaphylactic shock
• Dissemination of daughter cysts

C) Angioembolization is the treatment of choice ❌

Angioembolization is used for: bleeding tumors / vascular lesions / trauma

Hydatid cyst is a parasitic cyst, not vascular.

| Sign | Meaning

| ---- | -------

| Water lily sign | Floating detached membrane

| Daughter cysts | Multiple cysts inside mother cyst

| Hydatid sand | Parasite debris

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman presents with repeated episodes of fever, vomiting, and right upper abdominal pain radiating toward the neck. On clinical examination, Murphy’s sign is positive. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The constellation of right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain, fever, and vomiting in a middle-aged female is highly indicative of biliary disease. The pathognomonic clinical finding provided is a positive Murphy’s sign, where the patient experiences a sudden cessation of inspiration due to pain when the gallbladder is palpated during a deep breath. This sign is highly sensitive for acute cholecystitis. Gallbladder carcinoma (Option B) typically presents with chronic pain, jaundice, or a palpable mass rather than acute inflammation. Peptic ulcer disease (Option C) usually causes epigastric pain related to meals and does not present with a Murphy's sign. While acute appendicitis (Option D) can sometimes present with RUQ pain in cases of a retrocaecal or subhepatic appendix, Murphy's sign specifically targets gallbladder inflammation. The radiation of pain to the neck or shoulder is due to phrenic nerve irritation. Consequently, the clinical evidence points decisively toward acute cholecystitis as the primary diagnosis requiring further ultrasound verification and management

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which hormone is responsible for producing the characteristic ferning pattern seen when cervical mucus dries?
questions.explanation: The "ferning pattern" refers to the microscopic appearance of cervical mucus when it is allowed to dry on a glass slide. This pattern, which resembles the leaves of a fern, is caused by high concentrations of sodium chloride in the mucus. This phenomenon is exclusively under the influence of Estrogen (Option A) and is most prominent during the mid-cycle (pre-ovulatory) phase. Progesterone (Option B), which dominates the luteal phase after ovulation, inhibits the ferning pattern and causes the mucus to become thick and cellular (beading). This is known as a negative fern test. Prolactin (Option C) and 17-ketosteroids (Option D) (adrenal androgens) do not have a direct effect on the crystallization properties of cervical mucus. The presence of ferning is a reliable clinical indicator of estrogenic activity and is used to monitor follicular development and determine the timing of ovulation in infertility assessments
questions.learning: The "ferning pattern" refers to the microscopic appearance of cervical mucus when it is allowed to dry on a glass slide. This pattern, which resembles the leaves of a fern, is caused by high concentrations of sodium chloride in the mucus.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is associated with CSF otorrhea?
options: Traumatic rupture of the tympanic membrane
Fracture of the roof of the nose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Battle sign

A battle sign is seen in CSF otorrhea.

Battle sign refers to the retro auricular or mastoid ecchymosis that typically results from fracture of the middle cranial fossa following head trauma. It is prominent when there is a fracture of the temporal bone. CSF leak is associated with head trauma and fracture of the temporal bone. It can present as CSF otorrhea or CSF rhinorrhea or both.

Signs in basilar skull fractures:

* Hemotympanum: Pooling of blood behind the tympanic membrane, associated with fracture of the temporal bone. It is one of the earliest signs of basilar fracture.

* Periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes): Pooling of blood surrounding the eyes, associated with fractures of the anterior cranial fossa.

* Retroauricular or mastoid ecchymosis (Battle sign): Pooled blood behind the ears in the mastoid region is associated with fractures to the middle cranial fossa.

* CSF rhinorrhea or otorrhea: Double target sign, a double-ring pattern described with CSF-containing bloody fluid from the ear or nose, when dripped onto paper or linen.

Spontaneous resolution is seen within 14 days. Perioperative fluorescein cisternography is used for identifying the site of leakage. Persistent CSF leaks and large tegmen defects are treated with surgery due to the risk of herniation of the meninges and the brain.

Pearl PF1086: Features of CSF rhinorrhea

* Reservoir sign - In CSF rhinorrhea, the fluid which had collected in the sinuses, particularly sphenoid, empties into the nose.

* Double target sign or Halo sign or Target sign - CSF is mixed with blood and collected on a piece of filter paper. It shows a central red spot (blood) and a peripheral lighter halo.

* CSF can’t be sniffed back.

* CSF doesn’t stiffen the handkerchief.

Note: Reservoir sign is also seen in acute mastoiditis/ coalescent mastoiditis where mastoid acts as a reservoir of pus and pus reappear in EAC immediately after cleaning.
questions.learning: Battle sign — A battle sign is seen in CSF otorrhea. Battle sign refers to the retro auricular or mastoid ecchymosis that typically results from fracture of the middle cranial fossa following head trauma.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 9-year-old boy comes with complaints of right ear pain, difficulty in opening the mouth, painful swallowing, and fever. The oral cavity examination reveals the following. The external facial examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Quinsy

The given clinical scenario describes a child with fever, otalgia, trismus, and odynophagia with a normal external facial examination. The oral cavity shows congested and edematous tonsil and tonsillar pillars with edematous uvula pushed to the opposite side. These findings are highly suggestive of quinsy (peritonsillar abscess).

It is the collection of pus in the peritonsillar space between the fibrous capsule of the tonsil and the superior constrictor muscles of the pharynx. Both aerobic and anaerobic organisms are seen.

Patient presents with fever, unilateral throat pain, odynophagia, hot potato voice, torticollis, foul breath, referred otalgia through glossopharyngeal nerve and trismus due to spasm of pterygoid muscles.

Oral cavity examination may show congested and edematous tonsils, pillars, and soft palate on the involved side. Edematous uvula pushed to the opposite side. Pus may be seen on the tonsillar region. Jugulodigastric lymph nodes may be enlarged.

The management of quinsy is by antibiotics and incision and drainage to drain the abscess followed by interval tonsillectomy 4 to 6 weeks later.

Rare complications seen are parapharyngeal abscess, edema of the larynx, septicemia, lung abscess, or jugular vein thrombosis.

Other options:

Option A: Pharyngitis presents with fever, throat pain, enlarged tonsils, and lymphoid follicles on the posterior pharyngeal wall.

Option B: Parotid abscess occurs due to the suppuration of parotid space. It presents with swelling, redness, firmness, and tenderness in the parotid area and at the angle of the mandible. It is usually unilateral, but bilateral abscesses can occur. Due to the thick capsule, fluctuation is often difficult to elicit.

Option C: Bezold abscess is a complication of acute otomastoiditis where the infection/pus breaks through the thin medial side of the tip of the mastoid and presents as a swelling in the upper part of the neck.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which diagnostic technique is the best to assess renal perfusion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MAG-3 (Mercaptoacetyltriglycine)

The best diagnostic technique to assess renal perfusion is the MAG-3 (Mercaptoacetyltriglycine) or DTPA (Diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid) scan.

These are nuclear medicine imaging tests that help evaluate the functional and perfusion aspects of the kidneys. These scans involve injecting a radiopharmaceutical into the bloodstream, which is then filtered by the kidneys. The scan tracks the movement of the radiopharmaceutical through the kidneys, allowing the medical professional to assess renal blood flow, perfusion, and overall kidney function.

Other Options:

Option B- DMSA (Dimercaptosuccinic acid) scan is used to assess renal cortical morphology and function. It is commonly used to evaluate scarring or infection in the kidneys.

Option C- RGU is a radiographic technique used to visualize the urethra and bladder. It is primarily used to diagnose urethral obstructions and other structural abnormalities of the urinary tract.

Option D- CT urography is used to visualize the urinary tract, including the kidneys, ureters, and bladder. It provides detailed anatomical information but does not focus specifically on assessing renal perfusion.
questions.learning: MAG-3 (Mercaptoacetyltriglycine) — The best diagnostic technique to assess renal perfusion is the MAG-3 (Mercaptoacetyltriglycine) or DTPA (Diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid) scan.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a hyper-estrogenic condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Low BMI

Low body mass index (BMI) is not a hyper-estrogenic condition. In fact, low BMI can lead to decreased estrogen levels, as body fat plays a role in estrogen production.

Hyper-estrogenic conditions refer to conditions where there is an excessive level of estrogen in the body.

Estrogen is a hormone that plays a key role in the development of female sexual characteristics and the regulation of the menstrual cycle.

Other options:

* Some specific subtypes of ovarian tumors, such as Granulosa Cell Tumors and Sertoli-Leydig Cell Tumors, can produce excess estrogen, leading to hyper-estrogenic effects. However, the majority of ovarian cancers are not typically associated with hyper-estrogenic conditions.

* Tamoxifen is a medication often used in the treatment of estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer. It acts as a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM), blocking estrogen receptors. It acts as an estrogen antagonist in the breast and an estrogen agonist in the endometrium.

* Endometriosis involves the growth of tissue similar to the lining of the uterus (endometrium) outside the uterus. It's often associated with estrogen, as estrogen can stimulate the growth of endometrial tissue.
questions.learning: Low BMI Low body mass index (BMI) is not a hyper-estrogenic condition. In fact, low BMI can lead to decreased estrogen levels, as body fat plays a role in estrogen production.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A pregnant woman with a history of bronchial asthma is in the third stage of labor. Which of the following drugs should be avoided in the management of postpartum hemorrhage in this mother?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Carboprost

The drug that should be avoided in the management of postpartum hemorrhage in this mother with a history of bronchial asthma is carboprost.

Carboprost is an analog of PGF2α. It is used in obstetrics to induce second-trimester abortions and to control postpartum hemorrhage. Vomiting, diarrhea, and bronchoconstriction can occur.

Contraindications of carboprost:

Absolute
Relative

• Asthma
• Pulmonary hypertension
• Suspected amniotic fluid embolism

• Pre-eclampsia
• Renal disease
• Liver disease
• Heart disease

Other options :

Option B: Oxytocin is the first-line drug to prevent and treat PPH according to WHO guidelines. It is administered by intravenous route and may lead to hypotension and reflex tachycardia.

Option C: Dinoprostone is a prostaglandin E2 analog used for cervical ripening, induction of labor, and in atony treatment. It should be avoided in patients with a history of asthma, glaucoma, or myocardial infarction. One major adverse effect is uterine hyperstimulation.

Option D: Ergot derivatives are used in the control of postpartum uterine bleeding. It is given intramuscularly and is effective within 1–5 minutes. It is given at the time of delivery of the placenta or immediately after if bleeding is significant. Side effects are gastrointestinal disturbances like diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting.
questions.learning: Carboprost — The drug that should be avoided in the management of postpartum hemorrhage in this mother with a history of bronchial asthma is carboprost.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: In a patient presented with a fever and a positive filarial antigen test, what is the next appropriate method of management?
options: Detection of microfilariae in the blood smear
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Detection of microfilariae in the blood smear

A patient with fever and filarial antigen test positive is suggestive of filariasis. The next most appropriate step for this patient is the detection of microfilariae in the blood smear.

Classical filariasis occurs due to the obstruction of lymphatics by the adult worms, which results in lymph stasis. The disease initially causes acute attacks of lymphangitis and lymphadenitis. As time goes by the lymphedema worsens and is associated with the thickening of the skin and fibrosis of lymph vessels or blockage by adult worms. The lymphatic vessels of the male genitalia are most commonly affected in bancroftian filariasis, producing episodic funiculitis, epididymitis, and orchitis. Hydrocele or elephantiasis is a very common sign of chronic bancroftian filariasis.

The standard method for diagnosing active infection is the identification of microfilariae in a blood smear by microscopic examination. The microfilariae that cause lymphatic filariasis circulate in the blood at night showing a nocturnal periodicity. Microfilariae can be detected in blood smears of samples obtained at night between 10 PM to 2 AM. A thick smear should be made and stained with Giemsa or hematoxylin and eosin. For increased sensitivity, concentration techniques like membrane filter concentration can be used.

DEC provocation test (Option B) refers to the administration of Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) at a dose of 100 mg or 2 mg/kg body weight orally and subsequently collecting blood samples. This causes the mobilization of microfilariae into the peripheral blood and thus microfilariae can be detected 20-50 minutes after the DEC administration in the sample of peripheral blood.

Although the DEC provocation test has the advantage of blood sample collection even during day time, the guidelines from CDC, NVBDCP, and IAPSM suggest blood sample collection at night, followed by identification of microfilariae in a blood smear by microscopic examination as the standard method for diagnosis (Option C).

Methods to detect adult worms include:

• Lymph node biopsy to detect adult worms. Bone marrow biopsy is not a standard diagnostic procedure for filariasis, as adult worms typically reside in the lymphatic system rather than the bone marrow (Option A).
• X-ray (if worms are calcified)
• High-frequency ultrasound and doppler of the scrotum (Option D).

Serologic techniques provide an alternative to the microscopic detection of microfilariae for the diagnosis of lymphatic filariasis. Patients with active filarial infection typically have elevated levels of anti-filarial IgG4 in the blood and these can be detected using routine assays.

• Antigen detection by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and immunochromatographic test (ICT)
• Antibody detection tests have low sensitivity and specificity
• Molecular diagnosis is done by PCR (polymerase chain reaction). This test is positive only when microfilaria are present in peripheral blood. It is negative in chronic filariasis.

Diethylcarbamazine is the drug of choice. WHO has recently recommended a triple-drug combination of ivermectin, DEC, and albendazole as a faster and more effective alternative to expedite the elimination of filariasis.
questions.learning: Detection of microfilariae in the blood smear — A patient with fever and filarial antigen test positive is suggestive of filariasis. The next most appropriate step for this patient is the detection of microfilariae in the blood smear.

questions.text: Which genetic syndrome results from a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p deletion)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cri du chat syndrome

Cri du chat syndrome is caused by deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p deletion) and is characterized by a distinctive high-pitched “cat-like” cry in infancy.

• Genetic defect: deletion of 5p
• Clinical features:
• High-pitched cry
• Microcephaly
• Intellectual disability
• Hypertelorism and facial dysmorphism

Differentiation:

• Edward syndrome: trisomy 18
• Patau syndrome: trisomy 13
• Turner syndrome: monosomy X (45,X)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Once the diagnosis of gout is confirmed, which of the following medications—being a purine analog—is most appropriate for its management?
questions.explanation: Gout is a disease of hyperuricemia resulting in the deposition of monosodium urate crystals. For long-term management (urate-lowering therapy), the goal is to inhibit the enzyme xanthine oxidase. Allopurinol is the classic xanthine oxidase inhibitor and is chemically a purine analog (specifically an isomer of hypoxanthine). Because of its structure, it competitively inhibits the enzyme, reducing the production of uric acid. Febuxostat (Option D) is also a xanthine oxidase inhibitor but is a non-purine analog. Cytarabine (Option C) and Capecitabine (Option B) are pyrimidine analogs used in cancer chemotherapy and have no role in the management of gout. While Allopurinol is the most widely used agent, clinicians must be aware of its rare but serious hypersensitivity syndrome, particularly in patients with specific genetic markers like HLA-B5801. It is the standard-of-care purine analog for chronic gout prophylaxis
questions.learning: Gout is a disease of hyperuricemia resulting in the deposition of monosodium urate crystals. For long-term management (urate-lowering therapy), the goal is to inhibit the enzyme xanthine oxidase.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the device shown below?
options: It is used to measure infrared rays emitted by red blood cells
It is used for the localisation of calcified plaque
It is used to measure systolic blood pressure
It is used to measure blood flow and detect blood flow abnormalities in the blood vessel
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It is used to measure blood flow and detect blood flow abnormalities in the blood vessel

The given image is of a handheld doppler device. It is used to measure blood flow and detect blood flow abnormalities in the blood vessel.

The Doppler ultrasound device utilizes the doppler effect to assess the movement of red blood cells within blood vessels. The doppler effect is the change in frequency or wavelength of a wave in relation to an observer moving relative to the wave source. The device emits ultrasound waves that reflect off moving red blood cells. The frequency shift between the transmitted and received sound waves is used to calculate the velocity and direction of blood flow.

By analyzing these frequency shifts, the device can provide information about the speed and pattern of blood flow. This is particularly useful in detecting abnormalities such as blockages or stenosis.

Other options:

Option A: Doppler ultrasound does not measure infrared rays. Infrared measurements are typically related to thermal imaging or other specific applications unrelated to blood flow measurement.

Option B: Doppler ultrasound can help identify areas of reduced blood flow due to plaques, it is not specifically used for the localization of calcified plaque. Techniques like computed tomography (CT) or MRI are better suited for visualizing calcified plaques.

Option C: While Doppler can assist in certain vascular assessments, it is not a primary tool for measuring systolic or diastolic blood pressure.
questions.learning: It is used to measure blood flow and detect blood flow abnormalities in the blood vessel The given image is of a handheld doppler device. It is used to measure blood flow and detect blood flow abnormalities in the blood vessel.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: ADH acts through which aquaporin channel?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2

The antidiuretic hormone acts through aquaporin channel 2.

ADH binds to V2 receptors in the late distal tubules, collecting tubules, and collecting ducts, and stimulates the movement of an intracellular protein, called aquaporin-2 (AQP-2), to the luminal side of the cell membranes.
